Launched in 2035, it would overlap the fps development (2033-2040) by 5 years, against our 2-year cap, and add $3B of strain before discounting. Against hold it adds only +0.65 in S1 and S3, which is below our $1B tie band (epsilon), and it loses -2.99 in S2. A stable engine supply. Keep engine code 7. That gives CFM + P&W GTF2 (ready 2036) + Rolls-Royce UltraFan NB (ready 2037): three sources on the fps in 2040, 2045 and 2050, and three narrowbody engine makers in the market. The brief shows the enabler met. Do not change the code unless a maker proves not ready by EIS.

Hold course in the risk case. S3, covert Delay Tactics, costs the fps 5 percentage points of share for 5 years from EIS. The answer is supplier readiness (engines first) and keeping the workforce. It is never a rushed date or a cancellation.

Every Board item must stay above -$1B in each column, and S1, S2 and S3 all count as plausible. The plan must stay above -2.78 in the risk case (S3), which is Do Nothing's -0.78 less $2B. recommendations.text: Keep the fps whole and on plan. Hold the 2040 EIS and its headroom. Before the next stage gate, bring the Aerospace Safety Committee four things: written confirmation that MAX 7/10 certification is complete (still open from Round 1), the Chief Engineer's readiness view, the certification plan agreed with the FAA with no production-certification concurrency, and the stage-gate KPIs. If the plan has to move, reset it once and conservatively, never in serial slips. Do not cancel. A cancellation would write off about $30.16B ($60.32B x 5/10) with its debt penalty staying, and the fps is worth $17.55B to $18.99B more kept than cancelled in every column.

Hold the 787 Re-engine this round. Against the fps alone, a 2035 launch overlaps the fps development by 5 years (2035-2040) and adds $3B of strain before discounting. Its value is +0.65 in S1 and S3, below our $1B tie band, and -2.99 if Airbus re-engines the A350. Doing less and doing it better is the right call. If you expect S1 or S3, log the $0.65B as a doctrine premium, well inside the $2B cap. Bring the widebody case back in 2045, when it would not overlap the fps, and only if Airbus has not launched the A350 Re-engine by then (H3, second half).

Keep engine code 7. On the brief it fits CFM + P&W GTF2 (ready 2036) + Rolls-Royce UltraFan NB (ready 2037) at a 2040 EIS. That gives three sources in 2040, 2045 and 2050 and three narrowbody engine makers, and the enabler is met. CFM certifies first, and the others follow in sequence on durability evidence. Our Aerospace Safety Committee, which includes propulsion expertise, will ask for each maker's life-limited-part and durability status against EIS. Change the code before EIS only if a maker proves not ready, and never to fewer than two sources.

Debt stays first, and the cash peak is still ahead. Report the base and stress net-debt path every round. Programme cash runs $7.2B (2035), $8.4B (2036) and $7.8B (2037). By our computation from the brief, stress-case free cash flow falls to about $2.5B in 2036. Seek no new equity and keep the revolvers undrawn. Bring no dividend or buyback proposal before the fps cash peak is past and the rating is solidly investment grade. Those decisions are reserved to the Board, and the tracker's surplus-to-owners rule does not make them for us.

Prepare for the risk case without reacting to it. S3, covert Delay Tactics, costs the fps 5 percentage points of share for 5 years from EIS (worth $1.44B on the grid). Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot, engines first, since LEAP-1B remains the 737's sole source until the fps arrives. Report the supplier-shortages KPI at each stage gate and keep the retention and train-before-build measures. Report any supply or talent disruption to the Aerospace Safety Committee as a live problem. The response is a single conservative reset, never a cancellation.

Public statement and objectives. Add no new dates and do not answer Airbus's calendar. Reaffirm the plan, the FAA-first certification plan and debt first. Accept plainly that no order this round can lift narrowbody share before 2040: incumbency stays at 38% in 2040 and the 50/50 split is out of reach. Pay no objective premium for either.

frame.question:
We are five years into a ten-year fps. NGSA is due in 2037 and our EIS is 2040. Do we keep the plan whole and add nothing? Or does anything on this grid beat that by more than ε ($1B) inside the hard rules? Three parts:
(1) Is there any case for touching the fps? Cancel is barred by H5 and loses $17.55-18.99B. A reset needs evidence of a slip, and the brief shows none.
(2) Does a 2035 787 Re-engine belong in this round? It would overlap the fps by 5 years against H4's 2-year limit, and it is a bet on an A350 choice we cannot see.
(3) Does engine code 7 still give us three sources at a 2040 EIS, and is every maker on track for it?
Airbus's calendar does not enter it [B-2313].
frame.situation:
Decision year 2035.

**Our position.** The fps (10-year ramp, Solo) launched in 2030 and is in development, with EIS 2040 on plan. Code 7 is on record, and the brief fits CFM + P&W GTF2 (ready 2036) + RR UltraFan NB (ready 2037): 3 sources in 2040, 2045 and 2050. CFM's ducted engine is ready in 2036, and the CFM-Embraer partnership in 2037. NGSA is in development (EIS 2037), also on code 7, which is not a disallowed pair. The A350 has not been re-engined. The Rate Increase lapsed after 2030.

**Gates.** The brief reports no live quality, FAA, supply-chain or certification problem. So the KPI gate and the FAA-process gate are open, and there is no trigger for a reset.

**Grid** (S1 rivals hold / S2 Airbus launches A350 Re-engine / S3 risk case, covert Delay Tactics):
- fps hold + 787 hold (Do Nothing; continues the fps): +0.66 / -0.80 / -0.78
- fps hold + 787 Re-engine: +1.31 / -3.79 / -0.13
- cancel fps + 787 hold: -18.33 / -19.79 / -18.33
- cancel fps + 787 Re-engine: -16.66 / -21.76 / -16.66

**Differences:**
- The Re-engine adds +0.65 / -2.99 / +0.65.
- Keeping the fps instead of cancelling is worth +18.99 / +18.99 / +17.55 with the 787 on hold, and +17.97 / +17.97 / +16.53 beside a Re-engine.
- Delay Tactics would cost us $1.44B (S1 to S3). An A350 Re-engine costs our 787 $1.46B even if we hold.
- Malave's slip leg is S3. The floor is Do Nothing's -0.78 less $2B = -2.78.

**Debt.** Net debt has been $0 since 2029 (base) and 2030 (stress). The fps cash peak, the pig in the python, is still ahead of us. Programme cash is $7.2B (2035), $8.4B (2036), $7.8B (2037), $6.6B (2038) and $5.4B (2039). Base free cash flow is $8.07B, $7.12B and $7.53B in 2035-37. My reading of the tracker puts stress-case free cash flow at about $3.5B, $2.5B and $2.9B; Malave should confirm. The objective cell for both fps-kept rows is 2029 / yes / yes ($0.0B) / 3 (3). The cancel rows fall to 1 (1) engine source.

**Mission.** Debt repair and the engine enabler are met. Incumbency and 50/50 are not met: 38% in 2040 (the worst year), 43% in 2045, 47% in 2050. No order this round can lift narrowbody share. The Re-engine is widebody, the rate is hold only, and the fps cannot be accelerated. A cancel would only make share worse.

**Board risks** (its would-veto list; guidance, not red lines):
- any fps cancel, with or without a Re-engine;
- re787 launch: 5-year overlap, -2.99 in S2, +0.65 is below ε;
- any premium above $2B, or any premium not logged.

**Board items open from Round 1:**
- written confirmation that MAX 7/10 certification is complete;
- the Chief Engineer's readiness view;
- the certification plan agreed with the FAA, with no production-certification concurrency;
- each engine maker's durability status.
The Board's 2040 'in production' question is now answered by the brief: 3 sources counted in 2040.
levers_in_play: fps: hold (continue the 10-year to EIS 2040) | cancel (write-off $60.32B x 5/10 = $30.16B booked in 2035; its debt penalty stays). The ramp and form are fixed now. There is no launch option.

fps_engine_code: None or 1-7. Code 7 is on record. It does not change our payoff, but it decides the engine enabler. Brief table at EIS 2040: code 7 gives 3 sources (CFM + GTF2 + UltraFan NB), codes 5 and 6 give 2, codes 1-3 give 1. Change only if a maker proves not ready by EIS, and never to fewer than two.
rate_737: hold only. The Rate Increase was a 2030-only lever and lapsed. I accepted that loss in Round 1.

re787: hold | launch. Launched now: EIS 2040, $5B booked at EIS, $0.6B undiscounted debt penalty. Two-front strain is $3B x 5/5 = $3B undiscounted: Re-engine development 2035-40 against fps development 2033-40 on the board's strain measure.
Cancel of the 787 Re-engine: not in play, since none is launched.

Other moves (unpriced): KPI stage-gate governance of the fps; supplier readiness, engines first; workforce retention and train-before-build; engine durability reviews with each maker; the FAA certification plan; capital allocation (no shareholder returns before the cash peak is past; the Board reserves); widebody growth from Charleston capacity.
options_to_test: A. Continue: fps hold, code 7, rate hold, re787 hold. This is the Do Nothing row: +0.66 / -0.80 / -0.78. It is the baseline for every test. S3 sits $2.00B above the -2.78 floor by construction. Worst column -0.80 (S2). Objective cell 2029 / yes / yes ($0.0B) / 3 (3) in every column. My lean.

B. Continue + 787 Re-engine in 2035: +1.31 / -3.79 / -0.13. Against A: +0.65 / -2.99 / +0.65. It passes the slip leg (-0.13, $2.65B above the floor). But H4 strikes it (5-year overlap against a 2-year limit), its gain in S1 and S3 is inside ε, and it loses $2.99B in S2, beyond the Board's -$1B line. Objective cell unchanged at 2029 / yes / yes ($0.0B) / 3 (3). I test it only to put the row and the premium in front of the Board; it is not a live option.
C. Cancel fps + 787 hold: -18.33 / -19.79 / -18.33. Struck by H5. It fails the buffer by $15.55B, writes off $30.16B with the penalty staying, and cuts engine sources from 3 to 1. Closed.
D. Cancel fps + 787 Re-engine: -16.66 / -21.76 / -16.66. Struck by H5 (and the Re-engine grounds in B). It fails the buffer by $13.88B. Closed.

E. Engine code inside plan A: 7 (3 sources) against 6 (CFM + GTF2, 2), 5 (CFM + UltraFan NB, 2) and 3 (CFM, 1). Same payoff in every case. Code 7 keeps at least two sources even if one maker slips past 2040, so it is the resilient choice. I test it only against Pope's readiness and durability results.
red_lines: H1 and H3, first half (Round-1 rules): I ruled on both in 2030, with evidence. H1 was lifted; H3's first half no longer binds. Both are spent; neither is in force in 2035.
H2 cannot bind (EIS 2040). H7 has no trigger: the brief reports no crisis and no certification trouble.
H3, second half: no 787 Re-engine once Airbus has launched the A350 Re-engine. It has not fired, since the A350 is not re-engined. If it fires, the widebody option closes for the rest of the game.

H4: at most 2 years of overlap between a Solo fps and the 787 Re-engine. A 2035 Re-engine overlaps 5 years ($3B strain), so it is struck. The next legal round is 2045 (overlap 0), and only subject to H3.
H5: never cancel a launched fps. Both cancel rows are struck. If the plan has to move, one conservative reset, never serial slips [BX-1318, BX-1321].
H6: no Rate Increase under a live problem or as a reply to Airbus. Only hold is on offer.
H8: ties within ε ($1B) go to doctrine. Doctrine plus objective premium may total at most $2B, and every premium is logged.
Team rule: Malave vetoes any plan whose S3 (risk case) is below -2.78. The KPI doctrine vetoes a Rate Increase under a live problem (moot this round).

My own: no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263]; no fixed-price development, only cost-plus or risk-share [BX-1262, BX-1304]; never walk away from core customers' programmes [BX-1251]; one major development at a time [BX-1239, B-0341]; no blame on the FAA [BX-1323]; no attribution of a supplier problem to Airbus before exposure (doctrine); no new dates before the data supports them [BX-1268, B-2315].

On the compressed 10-year curve (0.60 / 0.90 / 1.15 / 1.35 / 1.00): stress 2.53 / 1.34 / 1.55 / 2.29 / 3.46. Lowest stress year 2036, headroom about $1.26-1.34B against $2.52B in A. Net debt stays $0.0B, so the brief's cell, yes ($0.0B), holds as I rebuild it. 2040: about $19.8B base and $15B stress, plus the Re-engine's widebody profit in S1, less in S2. B breaks if 2036 free cash flow falls about 43% below consensus, against about 52% for A.

tests.name: Full cost of a cancel (plans C and D)
tests.threshold: Write-off = bill x years elapsed / development years, booked in the cancel year; the debt penalty stays; cost it once, in full
tests.numbers: Write-off $60.32B x 5/10 = $30.16B in 2035, with the penalty staying. On the tracker's curve only $24.73B (41%) has actually been spent by 2034, but the board books the linear $30.16B. On the grid, keeping the fps is worth +18.99 / +18.99 / +17.55 (787 hold) and +17.97 / +17.97 / +16.53 (beside a Re-engine) in S1 / S2 / S3. Engine sources fall from 3 to 1 in the objective cell. H5 strikes both rows as well.

tests.name: Full cost of a slip in our own fps (CEO ask 6)
tests.threshold: One reset, owned at once, with buffer 'from a schedule and cost perspective'; cost the delay in full (concessions, rework, learning curve, carrying cost) (inference)
tests.numbers: No reset is on the table, and the grid has no column for an fps slip. If we ever had to reset, I would want the bill held at $60.32B, the cash moved right to flatten the 2036 $8.44B peak, and enough schedule and cost buffer to meet and beat the new date. All in, each year of slip on the brief's numbers would push the first fps profit year (+7.65 pre-tax in 2040, +$19.83B base free cash flow) a year right, add a year to NGSA's lead and so 1 pp to its lasting edge (NGSA 2037 with fps 2041 settles at 46/54, against 47/53 for 2040), and move the Delay Tactics window with it. Cost it once, never in serial slips.

tests.name: Capital allocation (CEO ask 4)
tests.threshold: No new equity; $10B of revolvers undrawn; no dividend or buyback before the fps cash peak is past and the rating is solidly investment grade; the Board reserves the call
tests.numbers: I agree. The tracker sends each year's surplus to owners once net debt is $0, so headroom does not build up. If the Board instead retained 2035-39 surplus, the cushion would reach about $17.48B under stress (3.47 + 2.52 + 2.94 + 3.83 + 4.72) and $40.47B in base, about twice the 2036 peak spend under stress. Earliest point to bring a proposal: once programme cash is falling after the 2036-37 peak, which is the Board's decision. Neither plan needs new equity or revolver draws.

tests.name: Rate step
tests.threshold: Only after stability and jointly agreed with the FAA; on the board, a 2030-only lever
tests.numbers: The brief offers rate_737: hold only. The Rate Increase lapsed after 2030.

tests.name: Premium in dollars (H8) and expected column (CEO ask 7)
tests.threshold: Report every doctrine or objective premium in $B; total at most $2B; name the condition that would break the number
tests.numbers: Expected column: S1, the CEO's read, with S2 close behind (I defer on Airbus). Holding the Re-engine: $0.65B in S1 (B +1.31 against A +0.66) or in S3 (-0.13 against -0.78), $0 in S2 (A is best by 2.99). It is logged as doctrine (H4, one development at a time). Keeping the fps: $0, since it is best in every column against cancel. Engine code 7: $0, since codes do not change payoff. Objective premium for share: $0, since no order this round can move narrowbody share. Total $0.65B, $1.35B inside the cap. What would break the plan: 2036 free cash flow more than about half below consensus, or a slip in our own fps, which the grid does not price.

tests.numbers: Plan A cell: 2029 / yes / yes ($0.0B) / 3 (3) in every column. Code 7 at EIS 2040 gives CFM + P&W GTF2 (ready 2036) + RR UltraFan NB (ready 2037): 3 sources. It also writes off $30.16B in 2035 with its penalty staying, and cuts engine sources from 3 to 1. Binding under the team rule (teams.md §9); the CEO revises within it. H5 strikes it as well.

The same $30.16B write-off applies, the penalty stays, and it leaves 1 engine source. Binding under the team rule; H5 strikes it too.

Against A it adds +0.65 / -2.99 / +0.65: inside epsilon in S1 and S3, and a $2.99B loss in S2. It lowers the worst column from -0.80 to -3.79. Its $5B lands at EIS 2040 beside the $60.32B fps bill. On the tracker, the $5B plus $3B of strain falls on the fps cash peak and cuts 2036 stress headroom from $2.52B to about $1.3B. I see no finance reason to open a second development now.

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
Five things would change my view:
(1) Pope reports a failing stage gate, or a slip in our own fps. I would then want one conservative reset: the bill held, the cash moved right, buffer from a schedule and cost perspective, the delay costed once and in full. Never a cancel.
(2) Free cash flow in the peak years runs far below the stress case. On my rebuild, A holds net debt at zero unless 2036 free cash flow falls about 52% below consensus. B gives way at about 43%.
(3) An engine maker proves not ready by the 2040 EIS. I would then back a code change, to no fewer than two sources.
(4) A later grid shows the 787 Re-engine clearing epsilon in the expected column, with no column below -$1B and no H4 overlap. That means the 2045 round at the earliest, and only if Airbus has not launched the A350 Re-engine.
(5) The Board retains surplus rather than distributing it. That would raise the stress cushion through the peak to about $17.5B. It changes the headroom, not the plan.
Nothing on this grid would lift my veto on the cancel rows: they sit $13.88-15.55B below the floor.
cfo.memo:
Kelly, I ran the slip leg as the baseline. S3 is the brief's labelled risk case, Delay Tactics. Do Nothing, which continues the fps, scores -0.78 there, so the floor is -2.78. Continue (A) passes by $2.00B; continue plus Re-engine (B) by $2.65B. Both cancel rows fall short: -18.33 and -16.66, $15.55B and $13.88B below the floor. My veto on them binds. A cancel would write off $30.16B in 2035, keep its penalty and leave us one engine source.

I confirm your cash read. The pig in the python is 2036: $8.44B of programme cash leaves free cash flow of $7.12B in the base case and $2.52B under stress; 2035 is $3.47B and 2037 $2.94B under stress. Net debt holds at zero, base and stress, through 2040, when free cash flow rises to about $14-15B even under stress.

On the Re-engine, my advice is hold. Its +0.65 sits inside epsilon, it loses $2.99B in S2, its $5B lands at 2040 beside the $60.32B fps bill, and with $3B of strain it roughly halves 2036 stress headroom, to about $1.3B. I log $0.65B of premium, inside the $2B cap.

No new equity, revolvers undrawn, and no dividend or buyback until the 2036-37 peak is behind us and the rating is solid: the Board's call.

This baseline lets us not only meet it but potentially beat it, barring free cash flow more than half below consensus in the peak year. Fully restoring the health of our balance sheet stays first.

tests.name: On-time, predictable delivery [record BX-1331, applied to airplanes by inference; slip prior is doctrine, profile.md §3]
tests.threshold: Can EIS 2040 be delivered as stated? Read the risk-case column (S3, Delay Tactics) and say how much of the plan's value depends on the nominal date.
tests.numbers: The brief has the fps (10-year, Solo, launched 2030) in development at year 5 of 10 with EIS 2040, unchanged. It reports no slip and no live quality, FAA or certification problem. Plan A (fps hold + 787 hold) scores +0.66 / -0.80 / -0.78, so Delay Tactics cost $1.44B from S1 to S3: 5 pp for 5 years from 2040, which is 25 point-years at about $0.058B of PV each. Keeping the fps instead of cancelling is worth +18.99 in S1 and +17.55 in S3, so 92.4% of its value survives the risk case. The 10-year date sits 3 years beyond a 7-year ramp's 2037. Against our clean-sheet slip prior of +2 to +5 years (doctrine; 787-8 May 2008 to September 2011 [B-0031, B-0526]), that is the headroom Ortberg asked about [BX-1275], and nothing in the brief has consumed it.

tests.name: fps stage gates at year 5 of 10 [doctrine BX-1259, BX-1263, BX-1309, B-0373] (CEO ask 2)
tests.threshold: KPI-based gates with no subjectivity; a certification plan agreed with the FAA; no production airplanes ahead of a mature, certifiable design; headroom kept. A failing gate means one conservative reset, never a cancel.
tests.numbers: This passes on what the brief carries, and no gate fails on the record. Spend to date on the tracker is $24.6B of $60.32B (2030-34: 3.0 / 4.2 / 4.8 / 6.0 / 6.6). Still to come is $35.4B over 2035-39 (7.2 / 8.4 / 7.8 / 6.6 / 5.4), with the cash peak in 2036 at 14% of the bill, $8.4B. By doctrine, R&D peaks 1-2 years before first delivery, about 2038-39 [B-0373]. The brief does not carry the design-maturity reading, the FAA plan's sign-off status or the Chief Engineer's readiness view. I will table those documents with the gate package for the Aerospace Safety Committee and will not invent them here. MAX 7/10 (Board item from Round 1): the brief is silent. Our last evidence is 'certification next year', from July 2025 [BX-1873]. No certification event appears on the record for 2026-34, and Boeing's observed share held at 40% every year, so I infer certification is complete (inference). Written confirmation is a programme document, not a brief number. No reset is triggered.

tests.name: Ramp choice, 7- or 10-year [inference on BX-1331]
tests.threshold: Which ramp can operations deliver predictably? State the strain and EIS of each.
tests.numbers: No ramp choice is open this round. The 10-year ramp launched in 2030 is fixed, and the brief offers only fps hold or cancel. The ramp in hand runs to EIS 2040 with $0 strain while re787 holds. Whether it can be delivered is reported under the on-time and stage-gate tests above, and both pass.

tests.name: Two-front strain, plan A (re787 hold) [doctrine B-0341, H4; arithmetic from dashboard_game.md §2] (CEO ask 3)
tests.threshold: A Solo fps and the 787 Re-engine overlap by at most 2 years. Strain is $3B × overlap ÷ 5 (fps from EIS-7 to EIS; Re-engine from EIS-5 to EIS). One major development at a time.
tests.numbers: With re787 at hold the overlap is 0 years and the strain is $0. The fps is the one major development [B-0341, BX-1239].

tests.name: Two-front strain, plan B (787 Re-engine launched in 2035) [doctrine B-0341, H4] (CEO ask 3)
tests.threshold: Same rule: overlap of at most 2 years.
tests.numbers: The Re-engine would be in development 2035-40 (EIS 2040) against the fps in 2033-40, an overlap of 5 years. Strain is $3B × 5/5 = $3.0B undiscounted, and the H4 limit is 2 years. The Re-engine's development would also run across the tracker's fps cash peak ($8.4B in 2036) and the doctrine's engineering peak (2038-39 [B-0373]). My answer to the CEO is no: engineering should not carry a widebody development on top of that. The grid shows the Re-engine adding +0.65 / -2.99 / +0.65, inside ε in S1 and S3. The next H4-legal round is 2045 (overlap 0), and only if Airbus has not launched the A350 Re-engine (H3, second half). The same failure applies to row D.

tests.name: Invest or partner on IP [record BX-1330, BX-1333; applied by inference]
tests.threshold: fps Solo where Boeing owns the airframe IP. A partner only if it adds what Boeing lacks.
tests.numbers: No partner option is on the board this round, and the fps is launched Solo with the airframe IP ours. The CFM-Embraer partnership (ready 2037) is CFM's move and changes no Boeing order. Engine makers come in on risk-share or cost-plus terms, never fixed price [BX-1262, BX-1304]. That is how we partner on what we do not make.

tests.name: KPI gate for the Rate Increase, my veto [doctrine B-2221, B-2351, B-2308, B-2283; not my record] (CEO ask 1)
tests.threshold: No Rate Increase while a quality, FAA or supply-chain problem is live. Steps of 5, KPI-gated, at least 6 months apart. Supplier readiness is a hard gate.
tests.numbers: My veto has nothing to bind on, for two reasons: rate_737 is hold only (the Rate Increase was a 2030-only lever and has lapsed), and the brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. The observed record shows Boeing at 40.0% of narrowbody deliveries (800 a year) and 58.8% of widebody (100 a year) in every year 2026-34, with no disruption. I read the 737 line as stable at its FAA-agreed rate and the 787 at its Charleston rate (inference). The brief gives no monthly rate, and our last evidence is 47 cleared in May 2026 [BG-0069]. The six FAA-agreed KPIs (rework, escapes, traveled work, supplier shortages, training, ticketing [B-2283]) are not reported as numbers in the brief, and none is flagged.

tests.name: Supplier readiness, engines first [doctrine B-2308, B-1449, BX-1243, B-2330, B-2043] (CEO ask 4)
tests.threshold: No live supply-chain problem. Supplier-shortages KPI not flagged. Fragile suppliers funded and kept hot through the risk window, so the fps ramp does not destabilise the 737 or 787.
tests.numbers: This passes on the brief: no supply-chain problem is reported, and the shortages KPI is not flagged, though its value is not in the brief. Keep these funded and hot: (1) CFM LEAP-1B, the 737's sole source until the fps arrives [B-1449]; (2) CFM as the fps launch engine; (3) GTF2 and UltraFan NB through durability testing; (4) any supplier flagged on the shortages KPI. The ladder runs: embed staff, buffer [B-2043], keep them above our rate [BX-1243, B-2330], requalify, fund, acquire. Exposure if Airbus orders a bottleneck, poaching or both: 5 pp for 5 years from 2040, $1.44B on the grid. The answer is buffers and hot suppliers, never a rushed date or a cancel.

tests.name: Engine readiness against a 2040 EIS, and the engine code [inference; doctrine BX-1298, BX-1264, BX-1325] (CEO ask 5)
tests.threshold: Each maker ready by EIS with durability margin. The code keeps at least two sources even if one maker slips. CFM certifies first, and the others follow in sequence on durability evidence.
tests.numbers: Ready dates on the public record: CFM ducted 2036, P&W GTF2 2036 and RR UltraFan NB 2037, so 4, 4 and 3 years of margin before 2040. The brief's code table at EIS 2040: code 7 gives CFM + GTF2 + UltraFan NB (3 sources in 2040, 2045 and 2050). Codes 5 and 6 give 2, codes 1-3 give 1, and code 4 (Joint Venture not formed) gives GTF2 + UltraFan NB, which drops our CFM baseline. Under code 7, if any one maker slips past 2040, 2 sources remain; under 5 or 6 a slip leaves 1. NGSA is also on code 7, which is not a disallowed pair. Durability: the brief carries no test data. P&W has stated publicly that every life-limited part will be at full life at EIS, validated in severe-environment testing, and that the date moves before the testing does. RR says support will be in place before EIS. The Committee should review each maker's life-limited-part status against EIS [BX-1298]. CFM capacity is the watch item, unpriced: it is on both new narrowbodies, the Embraer partnership (2037), LEAP on the 737 and A320neo, and the aftermarket [BX-1264, BX-1325]. No maker is shown at risk of missing 2040. I recommend keeping code 7.

tests.name: Trained workforce: talent poaching in the risk case [doctrine BX-1314, BX-1258, B-0373] (CEO ask 7)
tests.threshold: The plan absorbs poaching or a bottleneck in S3 and still sits above Malave's -2.78 floor. Retention and train-before-build are in place before the engineering peak.
tests.numbers: Plan A's S3 is -0.78, $2.00B above the -2.78 floor. Talent poaching costs the same 5 pp for 5 years ($1.44B) as a bottleneck. The measures adopted in Round 1 stand as unpriced moves: one enterprise incentive [BX-1314], train before we build [BX-1258], and staged hiring toward the 2038-39 engineering peak [B-0373]. The brief carries no attrition or training data, so I report the measures as in place, not as measured.

tests.name: Capacity follows demand [inference on BX-1329] (CEO ask 8)
tests.threshold: Back a Rate Increase only where it adds value against the same plan without it in the expected column; otherwise not applicable.
tests.numbers: No Rate Increase is on offer. On the widebody, the board holds the 787 at 100 a year (58.8% of 170) through 2060 without a Re-engine, so Charleston growth is unpriced. I support it as KPI-gated production capacity where customer demand is visible [BX-1317, B-2336]. It is production, not a development, so it does not load fps engineering.

tests.name: Working capital and cash conversion [record BX-1327, BX-1332, BX-1326; applied by inference]
tests.threshold: For each option: when the bill lands and what it does to cash, as a number. The stress-case debt line must hold at $0.
tests.numbers: Plan A: consensus free cash flow implied at $13.76B, stress two-thirds of that at $9.17B. Stress free cash flow 2035-39 is 3.48 / 2.54 / 2.95 / 3.84 / 4.72, my arithmetic from the brief (Malave confirms). The low point is $2.54B in 2036, net debt holds at $0 in base and stress, and the cell reads 2029 / yes / yes ($0.0B) / 3 (3). Plan B: the Re-engine's $5B plus $3B of strain over 2035-39, spread evenly at 79%, takes about $1.26B a year more. Stress free cash flow falls to about $1.27B in 2036, still positive, so the brief's yes ($0.0B) holds (an approximation; the curve shape is Malave's). Cancel: a $30.16B write-off booked in 2035, with the penalty staying. It avoids $35.4B of 2035-39 programme cash, but debt is already repaired in every row, so that cash buys nothing on the objective, while it costs $17.55-18.99B of PV and cuts engine sources from 3 to 1. Sensitivity: each $1B booked at the 2040 EIS costs about $0.25B of PV at 2026 (10.5%).

vetoes.plan: rate_737: increase
vetoes.ground: KPI veto NOT invoked. A Rate Increase is not on offer this round (2030-only lever, lapsed), and the brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. Under the team rule (teams.md §9) my veto binds only under a live problem, so it has nothing to bind on.

vetoes.plan: fps hold + re787: launch (row B), and cancel fps + re787: launch (row D)
vetoes.ground: H4 hard-rule flag, not my veto. Re-engine development 2035-40 against fps development 2033-40 is a 5-year overlap, above the 2-year cap, with $3.0B of strain undiscounted. Against hold the Re-engine adds +0.65 / -2.99 / +0.65. The rule binds the CEO; the next legal round is 2045.

vetoes.plan: fps: cancel (rows C and D)
vetoes.ground: H5 hard-rule flag, not my veto. The fps is launched. Keeping it is worth +18.99 / +18.99 / +17.55 with the 787 at hold and +17.97 / +17.97 / +16.53 beside a Re-engine. A cancel writes off $30.16B in 2035 with the penalty staying, and cuts engine sources from 3 to 1. If a gate ever fails, the answer is one conservative reset.

vetoes.plan: fps_engine_code changed to give fewer than two sources (1, 2, 3; or 4, which drops CFM)
vetoes.ground: Advice, not binding. No maker is shown at risk of missing 2040 (ready 2036 / 2036 / 2037). Code 7 is the only code that keeps two sources if any one maker slips. Change the code only on evidence that a maker is not ready by EIS, and never below two sources.

ops.would_change_mind_if: Five things would change my mind. (1) A live quality, FAA or certification problem on the fps in the brief, or a stage-gate document showing an immature design, an FAA plan not agreed or production running ahead of certification. Then I would recommend one conservative reset of the EIS, never a cancel. (2) A maker's ready date moving past 2040 or failing durability testing. Then I would recommend a code with at least two ready sources (5 or 6), CFM first. (3) A live supply-chain problem on LEAP-1B or a flagged shortages KPI. That would move supplier funding up the ladder, and it would trigger my veto on any rate step if one were offered. (4) Malave's rebuilt stress path breaching $0 net debt through the 2036 peak. (5) For the widebody: in 2045 the overlap is 0, and with the A350 still not re-engined the Re-engine would pass my strain test. Nothing Airbus does this round changes my operating results.
ops.memo:
My record is Global Services, not Commercial Airplanes. Delivery and cash conversion are my record, applied by inference; the KPI, strain and supplier results run on Boeing's operations doctrine.

First and foremost, on-time predictable delivery. The fps is at year 5 of 10, EIS 2040 on plan, and the brief reports no live quality, FAA or certification problem. No gate fails, so nothing triggers a reset. Delay Tactics would cost $1.44B, about $0.06B per point-year of share; 92% of the fps's value survives the risk case.

Second, engineering capacity. Strain is $0 on hold. A 2035 Re-engine overlaps the fps by 5 years, $3B of strain, across our 2036 cash peak and the 2038-39 engineering peak. H4 strikes it; 2045 is the clean round.

Third, engines. CFM ducted and GTF2 are ready in 2036, UltraFan NB in 2037: three to four years of margin. Code 7 gives three sources, and still two if any one maker slips. Keep it.

Fourth, cash. Stress free cash flow bottoms at $2.54B in 2036; net debt holds at $0. Each $1B booked at 2040 costs about $0.25B of PV. A cancel saves $35.4B of cash that debt no longer needs, and destroys $17.55-18.99B of value.

And finally, my KPI veto has nothing to bind: the rate is hold only. Two items I cannot sign from the brief: MAX 7/10 written closure and the Chief Engineer's view. I will table both at the stage gate.

Orders: fps hold, code 7, rate hold, re787 hold.

other_moves.move: fps stage-gate package to the Aerospace Safety Committee
other_moves.detail: Before the next development stage gate, Pope's seat brings the Committee four documents: (1) the MAX 7/10 certification closure, in writing; (2) the Chief Engineer's readiness view; (3) the certification plan agreed with the FAA, with no production airplanes ahead of a mature, certifiable design [BX-1263, BX-1309]; (4) the stage-gate KPIs, measured on data with no subjectivity [BX-1259]. If any gate fails, I bring one conservative reset, owned at once [BX-1318, BX-1319]: the bill is held, the cash moves right and the schedule and cost buffer is costed once and in full. Never a cancel (H5).

other_moves.move: Engine durability reviews, with CFM certifying first
other_moves.detail: Code 7 is kept: CFM + P&W GTF2 + RR UltraFan NB. CFM is the baseline engine and certifies first. GTF2 (ready 2036) and UltraFan NB (ready 2037) follow in sequence on durability and life-limited-part evidence [BX-1298]. Each maker reports its durability status to the Committee at every gate. The code changes before EIS only if a maker proves not ready, and never to fewer than two sources. CFM capacity across both new narrowbodies, LEAP and the aftermarket is a watch item [BX-1264, BX-1325]. Development terms stay cost-plus or risk-share, never fixed price [BX-1262, BX-1304].

other_moves.move: Supplier readiness through the risk window, engines first
other_moves.detail: Fragile suppliers stay funded and are kept hot ahead of our rate [BX-1243, B-2330]: LEAP-1B (the 737's sole source until the fps arrives [B-1449]), CFM as the fps launch engine, GTF2 and UltraFan NB through durability testing, and any supplier flagged on the shortages KPI. We use buffers and embedded staff [B-2043]. The supplier-shortages KPI [B-2283] is reported at each gate. Any supply or talent disruption goes to the Committee as a live problem. We attribute nothing to any rival before exposure.

other_moves.move: Workforce retention and train-before-build
other_moves.detail: One enterprise incentive [BX-1314], train before we build [BX-1258], and staged hiring toward the fps engineering peak (about 2038-39 on doctrine [B-0373]). This is our answer to talent poaching in the risk case, which is worth $1.44B on the grid.

other_moves.move: Capital allocation: debt first through the fps cash peak
other_moves.detail: No new equity, and the $10B of revolvers stays undrawn. I recommend to the Board no dividend or buyback proposal before the 2036-37 programme cash peak is past and we are solidly investment grade [BX-1305, BX-0556]. I also recommend that the Board consider retaining 2035-39 surplus as liquidity through the peak. Malave puts the stress cushion at about $17.5B if it does. The decision is reserved to the Board.

other_moves.move: 787 growth from Charleston capacity; widebody case reviewed in 2045
other_moves.detail: The 787 grows from Charleston production capacity where customer demand is visible, KPI-gated [BX-1317, B-2336]. That is production, not a second development. The Re-engine case comes back as a review in the 2045 round, when it would not overlap the fps (H4), and only if the A350 has not been re-engined (H3, second half).

other_moves.move: 737 MAX and 787 customer commitment
other_moves.detail: Production stability on the 737 MAX and 787 lines comes first and is gated by KPIs. The new airplane is built for commonality with the 737 fleet, so that our customers' transition is planned, not forced [BX-1273, BX-1274].

decision.public_statement:
Five years ago we launched a new single-aisle airplane. Here is plainly where it stands. The development is on its plan, and that plan still has its headroom. We haven't built airplanes ahead of a mature design, and we won't. We're working the certification plan with the FAA one step at a time. The data decides our stage gates, not the calendar. I'm not going to give you any new dates today.

The heaviest spending years on this airplane are in front of us. That's the pig in the python, and we planned for it. Debt stays first. The balance sheet is where it belongs, and we're going to keep it there through the peak.

On engines, CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce are all on this airplane. CFM certifies first, and the others follow on their durability evidence. Our customers and our production system both need more than one source of supply.

Our 737 MAX and 787 customers come first while we do this. Stable production and the KPIs set our rates, and we'll keep growing the 787 out of the capacity we've built in Charleston. We still develop with our suppliers on cost-plus and risk-share terms, not fixed price.

I think we're turning it. I don't think it's turned. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast, and we still have a lot of work to do.
decision.rationale:
**Decision.** We change nothing on the board: fps hold (the 10-year fps continues to EIS 2040), engine code 7 resubmitted, rate_737 hold and re787 hold. Every order is a default. Code 7 matches the code on record, and the Board never vetoes a code. So no item goes to the Board as a change. The submitted row and the default row are the same: fps hold + 787 hold, +0.66 / -0.80 / -0.78 (S1 / S2 / S3). My expected column is S1; the risk case is S3.

**Team rule, applied.**
(1) **Malave's buffer test (slip leg).** S3 is the brief's labelled risk case, and the floor is Do Nothing's -0.78 less $2B, or -2.78.
- A (hold/hold): -0.78, which passes by $2.00B.
- B (hold + Re-engine): -0.13, which passes by $2.65B.
- C (cancel + hold): -18.33, which fails by $15.55B.
- D (cancel + Re-engine): -16.66, which fails by $13.88B.
His veto on C and D binds, and I take it. H5 strikes them anyway.
(2) **KPI doctrine.** The rate is hold only, and the brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. Pope's veto has nothing to bind on.
(3) **Everything else is mine.** The only live choice was A against B.

**My four questions.**
- **Are the KPIs stable?** Yes. The brief reports no live problem, and observed shares have been flat at 40.0% NB and 58.8% WB through 2034.
- **Are market, technology and balance sheet ready?** Yes. Net debt has been $0 since 2029 (base) and 2030 (stress). Malave's stress free cash flow bottoms at $2.52B in 2036, the pig in the python, and net debt holds at $0 through 2040.
- **What if certification takes longer than we think?** On S3, A passes. The grid has no column for our own slip, so I asked for the reset rule in advance: one reset, the bill held, the cash moved right, costed once in full.
- **Is this doing less, better?** Yes. A is Do Nothing.

**Rulings.**
- **H5:** no cancel. Keeping the fps is worth +18.99 / +18.99 / +17.55 against cancelling (787 hold). A cancel would write off $60.32B x 5/10 = $30.16B in 2035 with its debt penalty staying, and it would cut engine sources from 3 to 1. If a gate ever fails, the answer is one conservative reset.
- **H4:** a 2035 787 Re-engine (development 2035-40) overlaps the fps development (2033-40) by 5 years, against a 2-year limit, with $3B of undiscounted strain. B is struck. Even without H4 it would lose:
  - its gain against A is +0.65 / -2.99 / +0.65, inside ε in S1 and S3;
  - it lowers the worst column from -0.80 to -3.79;
  - it roughly halves 2036 stress headroom, from $2.52B to about $1.3B (Malave);
  - on a probability-weighted view, A beats B whenever S2 carries more than about 18% weight (0.65 / 3.64), and the bulletin has not ruled out an A350 Re-engine.
- **H3, second half:** not fired, since the A350 has not been re-engined. If Airbus launches the A350 Re-engine, the 787 Re-engine option closes for the rest of the game. Otherwise the next H4-legal round is 2045 (overlap 0), and it comes back there as a review.
- **H1 and H3, first half:** ruled on in 2030 and spent. H2 cannot bind. H6 is moot. H7 has no trigger: no certification trouble is reported, so the FAA-process gate is open.

**Expected column and best grid plan.** I expect S1. Airbus said publicly that the A320neo and A350 stay its priority until NGSA enters service, and that it builds 'one well-prepared programme at a time'. S2 is close behind. The best grid plan in S1 is fps hold + 787 Re-engine at +1.31, which H4 strikes. A scores +0.66, $0.65B behind and within ε. Doing less and doing it better [BX-1239], and the higher-confidence plan with the higher worst column [BX-0548], settle the tie. In S2, A is best outright.

**Premium (H8), logged.**
- Doctrine premium: $0.65B, for holding the Re-engine (H4, one development at a time).
- Objective premium: $0. No order this round moves narrowbody share.
- Engine code 7 and keeping the fps: $0 each.
- Total: $0.65B, inside the $2B cap.

**Engine code.** Code 7 rests on doctrine, not my record (Low: I have no statement as Boeing CEO on engine selection). Its fitted sources are:
- at EIS 2040: CFM + P&W GTF2 (ready 2036) + RR UltraFan NB (ready 2037), three sources;
- in 2045 and 2050: the same three, with three narrowbody engine makers in the market.

Codes 5 and 6 give 2 sources and codes 1-3 give 1. Only code 7 still leaves two if any one maker slips past 2040. NGSA is also on code 7, which is not a disallowed pair.

**Where doctrine drove the choice.**
- the engine code;
- the strain arithmetic and the H4 limit;
- supplier-ladder detail.

**Where my record drove it.**
- debt first [BX-1305];
- doing less [BX-1239];
- one reset and never a cancel [BX-1318, BX-1321, BX-1251];
- no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263].

**Cash path (Malave, confirmed).**
- Programme cash: $7.24B (2035), $8.44B (2036), $7.84B (2037), $6.64B (2038) and $5.43B (2039).
- Base free cash flow: 8.07 / 7.12 / 7.53 / 8.43 / 9.32.
- Stress free cash flow: 3.47 / 2.52 / 2.94 / 3.83 / 4.72.
- Net debt: $0.0B every year, base and stress. A breaks only if 2036 free cash flow falls about 52% below consensus.
- The grid already nets the debt penalty (10-year fps $19.1B undiscounted, for scale), so it is not subtracted again.

**Open Board items.**
- MAX 7/10 closure: the brief is silent. Our last evidence is 'certification next year' (2025) [BX-1873], and I still treat it as done by inference. Pope's seat tables the written closure at the gate; I won't claim a document the brief doesn't carry.
- The Chief Engineer's readiness view and the FAA-agreed plan come in the same package.
- Each engine maker's durability status comes through the durability reviews.

final.public_statement:
Five years ago we launched a new single-aisle airplane. Here is plainly where it stands. The development is on its plan, and that plan still has its headroom. We haven't built airplanes ahead of a mature design, and we won't. We're working the certification plan with the FAA one step at a time. The data decides our stage gates, not the calendar. I'm not going to give you any new dates today.

The heaviest spending years on this airplane are in front of us. That's the pig in the python, and we planned for it. Debt stays first. The balance sheet is where it belongs, and we're going to keep it there through the peak.

On engines, CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce are all on this airplane. CFM certifies first, and the others follow on their durability evidence. Our customers and our production system both need more than one source of supply.

Our 737 MAX and 787 customers come first while we do this. Stable production and the KPIs set our rates, and we'll keep growing the 787 out of the capacity we've built in Charleston. We still develop with our suppliers on cost-plus and risk-share terms, not fixed price.

I think we're turning it. I don't think it's turned. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast, and we still have a lot of work to do.

- **H1 and H3, first half:** ruled on in 2030 and spent. H2 cannot bind. H6 is moot. H7 has no trigger: no certification trouble is reported, so the FAA-process gate is open.

**Expected column and best grid plan.** I expect S1. Airbus said publicly that the A320neo and A350 stay its priority until NGSA enters service, and that it builds 'one well-prepared programme at a time'. S2 is close behind. The best grid plan in S1 is fps hold + 787 Re-engine at +1.31, which H4 strikes. A scores +0.66, $0.65B behind and within ε. **Engine code.** Code 7 rests on doctrine, not my record (Low: I have no statement as Boeing CEO on engine selection). Its fitted sources are:

Codes 5 and 6 give 2 sources and codes 1-3 give 1. Only code 7 still leaves two if any one maker slips past 2040. NGSA is also on code 7, which is not a disallowed pair.

**Where doctrine drove the choice.**

**Where my record drove it.**

One programme at a time: keep the A350 Re-engine on hold this round. A 2035 launch runs at $6.67B a year in 2035-2036 against the $5.2B line. Bring it back in 2045, once NGSA spend has ended and it runs at about $1.0B a year, with a fresh grid and peak-cash test. It should come back only if no 787 Re-engine is on the public record. frame.situation:
BOEING AND THE PUBLIC RECORD (bulletin only).
- Boeing launched fps with the 10-year ramp in 2030, with entry into service planned for 2040. It selected code 7 with CFM as the baseline engine certifying first, on cost-plus or risk-share terms, with an FAA plan from day one.
- Boeing says debt comes first, returns stay off until it is solidly investment grade, and 737 MAX and 787 stability come first, gated by KPIs. It gives no further dates.
- No 787 Re-engine and no Rate Increase are on the record. GE's GEnx upgrade for the 787 has been ready since 2033.

ENGINE MAKERS.
- P&W GTF2 Solo: launched 2030, ready 2036.
- Rolls-Royce UltraFan NB Solo: launched 2030, ready 2037, which is zero margin to our EIS.
- CFM ducted engine: ready 2036. CFM-Embraer partnership: ready 2037.
- P&W made no Joint Venture commitment. Rolls-Royce keeps the Joint Venture door open and would commit once P&W does.

PROBLEMS REPORTED. The brief reports no supply crunch, no quality event and no technology or engine maturity slip. Observed shares have been flat since 2026: NB 60/40, WB 41.2%.

OUR POSITION.
- NGSA has been in development since 2030, with EIS 2037. On code 7 it is fitted with CFM + P&W GTF2 + Rolls-Royce UltraFan NB, 3 sources.
- ΔPV if nobody moves is +23.37 (S1) / +22.88 (S2), with yield 115.6%. The components are +39.13 NB operating profit, -15.23 programme investment at EIS and -0.53 debt penalty.
- Boeing's fps launch moved us from the S1 to the fps column of last round's grid. The plan is still positive in every column.
- Peak cash is $35.52B / 7 = $5.07B a year in 2035 and 2036, against the $5.2B line: $0.13B of headroom, 97% used. The $35.52B charge lands at EIS 2037.

OBJECTIVE STATUS (scored by the GM; it never changes the payoff).
- Defend 60/40: NOT met. NB share is 62% in 2040, 57% in 2045 and 53% in 2050. A three-year lead (2037 against 2040) sets a 53/47 long-run split. No option this round changes 2045 or 2050: Delay Tactics would act only in 2040-2044, and the A350 is widebody.
- Protect the A320 family: met at 60% before EIS.
- Enabler, dual or triple sources: met, 3 sources in 2040, 2045 and 2050 on every hold plan.
- Enabler, three NB makers in the market: met (CFM, P&W, Rolls-Royce in 2045 and 2050).
- Cancelling NGSA would drop the enabler to 2 sources.

THE BOARD'S GUIDANCE.
- It treats this as a consolidation round, risk-averse at 4 of 5.
- It wants NGSA held on its clock, code 7 kept, the A350 Re-engine on hold until 2045, and Delay Tactics at none, with the team's stricter condition left standing.
- No new programme cash in 2035-2036.
- It would veto an NGSA cancel, an A350 Re-engine launch, any Delay Tactics move and any combination of the two.

MY READ OF BOEING.
- Expected column: S1, rivals hold. A 787 Re-engine now would open a second front while fps is in development and debt comes first, and the GEnx upgrade already serves the 787.
- S2 (787 Re-engine) is not ruled out and is the worst plausible column: +22.88 on the hold plan.
- fps does not move NGSA: our own clock.

frame.asks_ops:
Lars, NGSA is two years from entry into service, and the Board wants your results directly. Please cover each point.

(1) FIVE PILLARS. Report your safety and quality results and any five-pillars flag, on our programmes and on any option above. Five-pillars flags and failures of your safety, quality, A320-ramp and supply-crunch tests are not overridable, by me or by the Board [AX-0073, AX-0081, AX-0015, AX-0056].

(2) RAMP AND SUPPLY.
- Confirm the A320 ramp shield and that there is no supply crunch. The brief reports none, and NB deliveries are flat at 1,200 a year [AX-0010, AX-0054].
- Confirm that engines and critical materials (titanium, rare earths) are secured for both families through the 2037 transition: the A320neo on CFM and GTF, and NGSA on three engines [AX-0060, AX-0062, AX-0063, A-0218].
- Confirm that our supply-security moves stay confined to our own ramp.

(3) NGSA PRODUCTION READINESS for EIS 2037. Is the wing buildable at rate, is the production system ready, and is anything slipping? A one-year slip would take us to 2038, outside 2035-2037. If you see it, re-time; never cancel.

(4) ENGINE CODE. This is the last round the code can change. I will take your supply recommendation unless it breaks a red line.
- Do you confirm code 7, with CFM certifying first, then GTF2 (ready 2036), then UltraFan NB (ready 2037, zero margin)?
- Give the integration and certification load of three engines on shared teams, for the Board's twice-yearly safety review.
- Assess UltraFan NB's zero margin to 2037 as a real-world risk the board does not price.
- Any reason to drop a maker? Neither is off track on the record.
- What happens to our sources and the three-maker count if P&W and Rolls-Royce form a Joint Venture this round?

(5) A350 RE-ENGINE, 2035. Run your tests:
- engineering capacity (2-year overlap, $1.2B strain);
- A350F and Spirit absorption [AX-0082, AX-0060];
- whether 2035 or 2045 better fits the production system, and rule 3 if a 787 Re-engine comes.
Cash is Thomas's call.

(6) DELAY TACTICS. Give your test on poaching: talent binds our own programmes [A-0366, A-0485], and there is the integrity pillar. Bottleneck and both are integrity flags, and the Board vetoes them. The team's stricter condition stands.

(7) OTHER MOVES, unpriced. Can we pursue A320neo delivery performance through the transition, and an A220-500 seat-size study (no launch cash in 2035-36), without drawing NGSA teams in its final two years?

(8) Tell me plainly whether your test passes or fails for each option. For each veto, say whether it is soft or rests on safety, quality, the A320 ramp or a supply crunch.

WHY, IN MY ORDER.
- Five pillars first: nothing covert, and safety leads the statement [AX-0081, AX-0073].
- Ramp: no new programme cash or engineering load in NGSA's last two spend years. A disciplined and controlled ramp of the A320neo and A350 until NGSA enters service [AX-0010, AX-0054].

GRID.

60/40. Not met (2050 at 53%), and no lever this round reaches 2045 or 2050. No PV, cash or integrity is traded for it.

PUBLIC LINE (draft register).
