It must be recorded as a Board item, together with his setting aside of the team's stricter condition, which he has kept standing. The Board's own Liquidity veto stands regardless.

vetoes.plan: delay_tactics: bottleneck
vetoes.ground: Five pillars (integrity): as chair of the Internal Control Committee I flag a first claim on scarce supply capacity aimed at a rival's programme; I could not defend it to the Audit Committee. It also fails peak cash at $5.27B. Not overridable.

vetoes.plan: delay_tactics: both (option 5), and any plan containing it
vetoes.ground: Company red line, rule 4: a second move. It is also an integrity flag (it contains bottleneck) and fails peak cash at $5.47B. The second $1B adds -0.47 in both columns. Not overridable.

vetoes.plan: rea350: launch + one Delay Tactics move (option 6)
vetoes.ground: Failed peak-cash test: $6.87B in 2035-2036, $1.67B over. The A350 Re-engine on top of one move is -1.22 in S2. Grid margin against the hold plan: +3.19 (S1) / +0.44 (S2), so the $1B bar is met in S1 only. Poaching carries the stricter-condition record; bottleneck in the mix is an integrity flag.

vetoes.plan: ngsa: cancel (option 7, any cancel row)
vetoes.ground: Company red line, rule 7: never cancel NGSA, and Boeing's fps is never a ground. Continuing gains $39.65B in both columns. The write-off is $25.37B in 2035, 4.9x one year's FCF. Not overridable.

cfo.would_change_mind_if: (1) An option that passes every test of mine and every red line shows at least $1B over the hold plan on the grid. None does: every higher row fails peak cash. (2) The Board decides otherwise. (3) The cash line moves on reported numbers, not on bank forecasts. One Delay Tactics move would pass at a reported FCF of €4.80bn or more, or at $1.11 per € or more, and only against the unrounded $5.23B. An A350 Re-engine alongside NGSA would need about €6.07bn. My record holds only FY2025's €4,753m, and I do not move the line on the bank run-rate. (4) NGSA itself fails my line if its bill passes $36.4B, FCF falls below €4.61bn or the rate falls below $1.068 per €. None is crossed. I would report the fail and margin, never cancel (rule 7). (5) The A350 Re-engine returns in 2045, when it runs at $1.0B a year with no overlap, provided no 787 Re-engine is on the record (rule 3) and the 2045 grid is positive in its worst plausible column. (6) If ramp cash stays near FY2025, the payout goes to the lower end of 30-50% in 2035-2036. At 48% the FY2025 base turns to net debt of about $2.3B in 2035. Engine code: no evidence of my own; I defer to Lars Wagner and expect code 7.
cfo.memo:
Board paper, round 2035: consolidation. CFO test on the hold plan: pass.

Liquidity. NGSA runs at $35.52B / 7 = $5.07B in 2035 and 2036, then nothing, against one year's free cash flow of €4,753m, about $5.2B at an assumed $1.10 [AX-0104]. Headroom: $0.13B. No added item fits. An A350 Re-engine gives $6.67B, one Delay Tactics move $5.27B, both moves $5.47B, and the A350 Re-engine with one move $6.87B. Each fails, and each fail is a binding soft veto.

Robustness. The worst plausible column is S2, at +22.88. The A350 Re-engine item is +1.54 / -1.21, worth $0.72-0.85B at a 25-30% chance of S2: under $1B. One move is +1.65 / +1.66. It clears the grid but not the cash line, and any override is the CEO's call. I would flag bottleneck and both to the Audit Committee [AX-0106].

Balance sheet. On the bank run-rate (context only), net cash still rises about $2.4B a year after NGSA and the dividend. On the FY2025 base it holds only at the lower end of the 30-50% payout; at 48% it turns to net debt in 2035 [AX-0102, AG-0058]. The guardrail stands: no equity raise, no dividend cut, no new return policy.

The 2037 charge. $35.52B lands against $18.3B of operating profit: reported -$17.2B. We lead with EBIT Adjusted and show the reported figure beside it [AX-0103]. No break-even is crossed.

Cancel: a red line, writing off $25.37B.

Orders: hold, code 7 (I defer to Lars Wagner), hold, none. No Board items.

tests.name: (1) Five pillars and quality: option 1, the hold plan (NGSA hold, code 7, A350 hold, Delay Tactics none)
tests.threshold: No order whose public explanation would contradict safety, quality, integrity, compliance or security, and nothing covert. A five-pillars failure is never overridden.
tests.numbers: Every order is a default, so nothing is covert and no order is a Board item. The brief reports no quality event and no safety issue. The public line can lead with safety, give windows rather than dates and say 'we intend to offer a choice of engines'. I raise no five-pillars flag on option 1. For the Board's twice-yearly safety review I report the unpriced load of integrating and certifying three engines in 2035-2037 (see test 4).

tests.name: (2a) A320 ramp shield: every option
tests.threshold: No new programme spend that competes with the open A320 ramp commitment (rate 70-75 by end-2027, stabilising at 75). On this board it passes unless the brief reports a ramp problem.
tests.numbers: 2035 is eight years past the end-2027 rate date. NB deliveries are flat at 1,200 a year (60.0% of 2,000) for 2026-2036, and the A320 family holds 60% in every year before NGSA enters service. The brief reports no ramp problem. Option 3 would add $1.00B + $0.60B strain a year in 2035-36, but that competes with NGSA and the cash line, not with an open A320 rate commitment, so the shield is not the ground against it.

tests.name: (2b) Supply crunch: every option
tests.threshold: If the brief reports a supply-chain crunch, no new concurrency
tests.numbers: The brief reports no supply crunch, no quality event and no maturity slip. Engines: A320neo stays on CFM and P&W GTF until NGSA EIS (rules.md). NGSA code 7 fits three engines. Critical materials: the board does not model titanium or rare earths, so I can only confirm that nothing on the record shows a shortage. The in-house work packages and the titanium and rare-earth de-risking continue (other move b), confined to our own production system and never aimed at a rival's supply chain. That is the legitimate form of a first claim on capacity.

tests.name: (3) NGSA production readiness for EIS 2037
tests.threshold: Launch only once the wing is buildable at rate and the production system has matured with the aircraft (proxy: launched in the 2028-2030 window). Red line, rule 1: no EIS before 2035. On a reported slip, re-time and never cancel.
tests.numbers: NGSA was launched in 2030, the last year of the window, and is on the record for EIS 2037, two years after the 2035 technology-ready year. The brief reports no technology or production slip, and the board has no injects, so it gives me no wing-at-rate data beyond the record. A one-year slip would put EIS in 2038. That breaks no red line, and the public window 'second half of the 2030s' still covers it, which is why we give windows. The answer would be to re-time, never to cancel. No re-timing is warranted on the record.

tests.name: (4) Engine supply and engine code: last round the code can change
tests.threshold: Keep CFM plus at least one second maker (code 5, 6 or 7; code 7 when it is unclear which will be ready by NGSA EIS). This is a recommendation, not a veto ground.
tests.numbers: I recommend code 7, confirmed. Readiness by NGSA EIS 2037: CFM always (ducted engine ready 2036, or a LEAP derivative); P&W GTF2 ready 2036, one year of margin; RR UltraFan NB ready 2037, zero margin. Code 7 fits 3 sources and gives the enabler 3 / 3 in 2040, 2045 and 2050 on every hold plan. Codes 5 and 6 give 2 sources, code 3 gives CFM alone, and codes 1, 2 and 4 drop CFM as a named source, so no. Neither maker is off track on the record, so I have no ground to drop one. Integration load (unpriced, for the safety review): three certification campaigns on shared teams in NGSA's last two years. The A320neo precedent is two engines certified six months apart (P&W Nov 2015, CFM May 2016). Mitigation: CFM certifies first and alone gates EIS, GTF2 follows, and UltraFan NB certifies last. UltraFan's zero margin is a real-world risk the board does not price: on the board an unready maker is simply dropped, but in practice it must never hold NGSA's EIS (rule 8). It follows in sequence after EIS if it needs to. Joint Venture this round: rules.md folds both solo programmes into it, and its engine would be ready no later than the further-along solo (2036). Code 7 still fits it, giving CFM + the Joint Venture engine = 2 sources, still dual. The brief does not give the maker count under a Joint Venture. rules.md gives P&W and RR equal NB shares, so I read it as 3 makers (inference; GM to confirm). Code 4 is never acceptable because it drops CFM.

tests.name: (5a) Engineering capacity: option 3, A350 Re-engine launched 2035 (EIS 2040)
tests.threshold: NGSA / A350 development overlap of 2 years or less ($1.2B strain), unless the grid shows at least $1B more. Red line, rule 6: one new launch per round.
tests.numbers: NGSA development runs 2030-2037 and the A350 Re-engine 2035-2040, so the overlap is 2035-2037 = 2 years, exactly at the limit. Strain is $3B x 2/5 = $1.2B ($0.6B a year in 2035-36). It is one launch this round, so rule 6 passes. The item is +1.54 (S1) / -1.21 (S2). Operating note, not a test failure: those two overlap years are the three-engine certification campaign and the production run-up to EIS 2037, and they draw on the same engineering talent [A-0366, A-0485]. Rule 3 does not bind, because no 787 Re-engine is on the record.

tests.name: (5b) A350F and Spirit absorption: option 3
tests.threshold: No A350 Re-engine while the A350F and the Spirit A350 packages are being absorbed. Proxy: not in round 1; round 2 (2035) at the earliest, the last year of the company window 2033-35.
tests.numbers: 2035 is the earliest round the proxy allows. Timing for the production system: a 2045 launch (EIS 2050) has zero overlap and zero strain, after NGSA EIS and after the three engine certifications, with the engineering teams free. Operationally I prefer 2045 to 2035. Rule 3: if Boeing launches a 787 Re-engine (S2), the A350 Re-engine is off for 2045 and we compete on price. Cash and what we forgo by waiting are Thomas's call.

tests.name: (6a) Delay Tactics, poaching: option 4
tests.threshold: Rule 4: at most one move, after fps is public and before its EIS. Rule 5: poaching only while an Airbus programme is in development. Five pillars. The team's stricter condition: the move must change who enters service first (it stands unless the CEO records setting it aside).
tests.numbers: Rule 4 passes: fps is public (launched 2030, EIS 2040), there was no earlier move, and it is one move. Rule 5 passes at the order: NGSA is in development through 2036. But $0.6B of the $1B ($0.20B a year over 2035-39) falls in 2037-39, when nothing of ours is in development, so the reading of poaching as recruitment for our own programmes weakens after 2036. On my profile's recruitment reading I raise no five-pillars flag; Toepfer (Internal Control) and the Board rule on integrity. It fails the team's stricter condition, which the CEO keeps standing: NGSA already enters service first (2037 against 2040), and the move shifts share in 2040-44, not EIS. The item is +1.65 (S1) / +1.66 (S2) against hold, which is the best passing option. It does nothing for 2045 or 2050. Unpriced: a talent fight in NGSA's last two years exposes our own attrition [A-0366].

tests.name: (6b) Delay Tactics, bottleneck or both: option 5 and any bottleneck
tests.threshold: Five pillars: a bottleneck is acceptable only as a first claim on scarce capacity for our own ramp. Rule 4: never a second move ('both' is two).
tests.numbers: The board's bottleneck move exists to delay fps (Boeing -5 pp for 5 years from 2040). That is more than a first claim for our own ramp, so it is an integrity breach. 'both' is two moves, which breaks rule 4. The second move adds -0.47 in both columns. The both row is +24.55 / +24.07, an item of +1.18 / +1.19. Our legitimate supply security is other move (b), confined to our own production system.

tests.name: (6c) Option 6: A350 Re-engine + one Delay Tactics move
tests.threshold: Each part on its own tests
tests.numbers: The A350 part passes my tests (2-year overlap, $1.2B strain). The Delay Tactics part fails as in 6a (poaching) or 6b (bottleneck or both). The row is +26.56 / +23.32, an item of +3.19 (S1) / +0.44 (S2) against hold. With both moves the row is +26.08 / +22.84, an item of +2.71 / -0.04.

tests.name: (7) Cancel NGSA: option 7
tests.threshold: Never cancel NGSA (company doctrine, rule 7). On an engine maturity slip, re-time.
tests.numbers: No slip is reported. A cancel writes off $35.52B x 5/7 = $25.37B in 2035. The item is -39.65 in both S1 and S2. It drops the enabler to 2 sources and leaves only the A320neo against fps from 2040.

tests.name: (8) Other moves: NGSA team draw in 2035-36
tests.threshold: No unpriced move draws NGSA engineering in its last two development years
tests.numbers: (f) A320neo delivery performance through the transition: yes. It is my line's core job and runs on the existing production teams. (g) A220-500 seat-size gap: a study only, with no launch cash in 2035-36, staffed outside the NGSA programme. Any launch decision comes after NGSA EIS and would count as a new launch under rule 6. (c) Sequential certification with CFM first: yes, as in test 4. (b) Own supply: yes, confined to our own ramp.

tests.name: Engine maturity slip
tests.threshold: If reported, re-time NGSA so EIS stays at or after the new technology-ready year; never cancel
tests.numbers: None is reported. GTF2 2036 and UltraFan NB 2037 are on track on the record. A slip of a single engine maker is handled by sequence (it follows after EIS), not by re-timing NGSA.

tests.name: Boeing Rate Increase
tests.threshold: No reaction: our own disciplined ramp
tests.numbers: None is on the record, and the lever was 2030-only.

vetoes.plan: Option 4: delay_tactics poaching (one move)
vetoes.ground: This is a programme test. The team's stricter Delay Tactics condition, which the CEO keeps standing, fails: NGSA already enters service first (2037 against fps 2040), and the move shifts share in 2040-44, not EIS. Rules 4 and 5 pass, and I raise no five-pillars flag on the profile's recruitment reading. The ground is not safety, quality, the A320 ramp or a supply crunch. The grid margin against the best passing option (hold) is +1.65 (S1) / +1.66 (S2). The veto binds while the condition stands. If Faury records setting the condition aside, the grid's $1B test stands in for it and this objection drops to a flag, provided that is recorded as a Board item. The Board's Liquidity veto ($5.27B against $5.2B) and the integrity ruling belong to Toepfer and the Board, not to me.

vetoes.plan: Option 5 and any bottleneck order: delay_tactics bottleneck or both
vetoes.ground: Five-pillars (integrity) breach. The bottleneck is designed to delay fps, which is more than a first claim on capacity for our own ramp. 'both' is a second move, which breaks red line rule 4. Not overridable by Faury or the Board. The 'both' item is +1.18 / +1.19, and the second move is -0.47 in both columns.

vetoes.plan: Option 6: A350 Re-engine + any Delay Tactics move
vetoes.ground: The veto rests on the Delay Tactics part: it is soft as in option 4 with poaching, and a pillars and rule 4 breach with bottleneck or both. The margin against hold is +3.19 (S1) / +0.44 (S2) with one move, and +2.71 / -0.04 with both. The A350 part passes my own tests.

vetoes.plan: Option 7: any ngsa cancel row
vetoes.ground: Company doctrine and red line: never cancel NGSA, and with no slip reported there is nothing to re-time. A $25.37B write-off in 2035 and an item of -39.65 in both columns, so no override is arithmetically possible. The enabler drops to 2 sources.

vetoes.plan: Option 3: rea350 launch in 2035 (flag only, no veto)
vetoes.ground: My capacity and A350F/Spirit tests pass at the limit: a 2-year overlap and $1.2B strain in 2035-36. I flag that those years carry three engine certifications and the run-up to NGSA EIS, so 2045 fits the production system better (zero overlap). I do not veto. Cash is Toepfer's test and the Board's.

ops.would_change_mind_if: (a) A supply crunch, a quality event or an NGSA production slip in the record. Then no new concurrency, and the A350 Re-engine would fail my capacity test too. A slip means re-time NGSA, never cancel. (b) Engine code: I would leave code 7 only on evidence that a named maker is off track for 2037, or that the third certification cannot run without pulling NGSA teams off CFM-first certification. Then I would move to code 6 (CFM + GTF2) and keep dual source. Never in reaction to Boeing. (c) A350 Re-engine: my tests already pass a 2035 launch at the limit. I would back a launch only if Toepfer's peak-cash line also passes. Otherwise 2045, once NGSA teams are free and no 787 Re-engine is on the record (rule 3). (d) Poaching: my objection drops to a flag if Faury records setting aside the team's stricter condition, which lets the grid's $1B test stand in (it clears at +1.65/+1.66). The Board's Liquidity and integrity tests still govern. Bottleneck and both: nothing changes my mind.
ops.memo:
Role-derived tests, Very low confidence: nothing of mine is on record.

Hold plan: pass on every test. No five-pillars flag, no quality event, no supply crunch reported. A320 ramp shield holds: 1,200 NB a year at 60% through 2036. NGSA stays on its record for EIS 2037, behind the 2035 technology year, with no slip reported. If one comes, re-time, never cancel; "second half of the 2030s" still covers 2038.

Engines, last call on the code: keep 7. CFM certifies first and gates EIS. GTF2 (ready 2036, one year of margin) follows, then UltraFan NB (2037, zero margin), which must never hold NGSA. Three sources, three makers through 2050. A P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture still fits code 7: two sources, still dual. Codes 1, 2 and 4 drop CFM.

A350 Re-engine in 2035: my tests pass, at the limit. Overlap 2035-2037 is two years, $1.2B strain; round 2 is the earliest the A350F and Spirit absorption allows. No veto from me. But those two years carry three engine certifications and the run to EIS. 2045 fits the production system better: zero overlap, teams free. Cash is Thomas's call.

Delay Tactics: poaching fails the team's stricter condition, which stands: NGSA already enters service first. Binding while it stands; margin +1.65/+1.66. Bottleneck and both: integrity breach, and both is two moves. Binding, no override.

Cancel: no. $25.37B written off, -39.65 in both columns, two sources.

A320neo delivery performance: yes. A220-500: study only, staffed outside NGSA.

other_moves.move: Engine-maker risk-sharing invitation, reworded
other_moves.detail: CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce remain selected on NGSA (code 7) and invited as risk-sharing partners. Airbus 'intends to offer a choice of engines'. This is not a promise: each maker is fitted once its engine is ready and certified, and nothing is said about dates. It takes up the Board's 2030 and 2035 recommendation. It is unpriced and supports the enabler (dual or triple sources, three narrowbody makers).

other_moves.move: Secure our own supply for the A320 family and the NGSA ramp
other_moves.detail: Continue to bring critical work packages in-house and to de-risk titanium and rare earths [AX-0060, AX-0061, AX-0062, AX-0063], confined to our own disciplined and controlled ramp through the 2037 transition. It is never aimed at a rival's supply chain. The Ethics, Compliance and Sustainability Committee stays informed, as the Board asked.

other_moves.move: Sequential engine certification, CFM first, and the last engine-code call
other_moves.detail: Wagner's mitigation, adopted. Code 7 is confirmed in the last round it can change. CFM integrates and certifies first and alone gates the 2037 entry into service. P&W GTF2 (ready 2036) follows, then Rolls-Royce UltraFan NB (ready 2037, zero margin), which is never allowed to hold NGSA's EIS and joins in sequence after EIS if it needs to. Wagner reports the three-engine integration and certification load, and UltraFan's zero margin, to the Board's twice-yearly safety review. If P&W and Rolls-Royce form a Joint Venture, code 7 fits its engine and supply stays dual (CFM + the Joint Venture engine).

other_moves.move: Payout guardrail and presentation of the 2037 charge
other_moves.detail: Toepfer's guardrail, adopted. Returns stay inside 30-50%, at the lower end in 2035-2036 if ramp cash stays near the FY2025 level (at 48% the FY2025 base would turn to net debt of about $2.3B in 2035). No equity raise, no dividend cut, no new return policy, and no new buyback beyond share-plan cover until NGSA spend ends. The $35.52B programme charge at the 2037 EIS is isolated as a programme item: EBIT Adjusted leads, with reported EBIT shown beside it. Whether the payout base is reported or adjusted earnings is a reserved Board matter for the 2037 budget. No internal long-term-plan targets are disclosed [AX-0005].

other_moves.move: A350 Re-engine review gate for 2045
other_moves.detail: The A350 Re-engine comes back at the 2045 round with a fresh grid and a fresh peak-cash test. On these bills it would run at $1.0B a year with zero overlap, 19% of the line. It comes back only if no 787 Re-engine is on the public record (rule 3) and its worst plausible column is positive. If Boeing launches a 787 Re-engine, we stay out and compete on price.

other_moves.move: A320neo delivery performance through the transition
other_moves.detail: Wagner's line: a disciplined and controlled ramp of the A320neo and A350 families and delivery performance for our customers until NGSA enters service, on the existing production teams. Unpriced.

other_moves.move: A220-500 seat-size study
other_moves.detail: A study only. There is no launch cash in 2035-2036, and it is staffed outside the NGSA programme. Any launch decision comes after NGSA EIS and would count as a new launch under rule 6. Unpriced.

other_moves.move: Zero-for-zero trade advocacy through industry coalitions
other_moves.detail: Keep working with industry partners, Boeing included, for a tariff-free aerospace trade regime [AX-0088, AX-0046].

decision.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft is in its final phase of development and remains on track for entry into service in the second half of the 2030s, on the clock we set when we prepared it. We intend to offer a choice of engines. CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce are all on the programme, and each engine will join the aircraft once its maturity and durability are proven: we will not compromise on certification. Until the new aircraft enters service, the A320neo and A350 families remain our priority, with a disciplined and controlled production ramp-up, delivery performance for our customers through the transition and continued work to secure our own supply chain, engines and critical materials first. We are funding the programme with financial discipline, within our financial flexibility and our existing shareholder return policy. We will continue to work with our industry partners for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for aerospace trade. Preparing the Airbus of the 2030s means one well-prepared programme at a time, for a stronger and more sovereign European aerospace industry.
decision.rationale:
DECISION BY THE TEAM RULE
Orders: ngsa hold, engine code 7 (unchanged, confirmed in its last changeable round), rea350 hold, delay_tactics none. No Board items. Row: +23.37 (S1) / +22.88 (S2). Probability-weighted at 25-30% S2: +23.22 to +23.25. I verified the grid items and the peak-cash arithmetic myself on the brief's numbers.

FRAMING, in my order
- Five pillars: nothing covert, and both colleagues raise no flag on this plan [AX-0081, AX-0073].
- Ramp: no new programme cash or engineering load in NGSA's last two spend years [AX-0010, AX-0054].
- Airbus of the 30s: NGSA whole, with entry into service in the second half of the decade and three engine sources [AX-0020, A-0409].
- Board: this is the Board's own expected package.

STEP 1: DELETE RED-LINE AND PILLAR BREACHES
- Every cancel row: rule 7. Continuing gains $39.65B in both columns. Cancelling writes off $25.37B in 2035 and drops the enabler to 2 sources. Boeing's fps is never a ground.
- Delay Tactics 'both', in any row: rule 4 (two moves), and an integrity flag from both colleagues.
- Any 'bottleneck': Toepfer (as chair of the Internal Control Committee) and Wagner both flag integrity, because the board's move exists to delay fps, not to give us a first claim for our own ramp. A pillars failure cannot be overridden.
- Left: the hold plan, + A350 Re-engine, + poaching, and + A350 Re-engine + poaching.

STEP 2: SURVIVORS OF BOTH TESTS
- Hold plan: passes both.
  - Toepfer: $5.07B in 2035-36 against $5.2B; worst column +22.88; the net-cash bridge holds under the guardrail; no break-even crossed.
  - Wagner: no pillars flag; A320 shield holds; no crunch; NGSA ready for 2037; code 7.
- + A350 Re-engine fails Toepfer twice: peak cash of $6.67B is $1.47B over the line, and the added item is -1.21 in S2. Both are binding soft vetoes. Wagner passes it at the limit but flags 2045 as the better fit.
- + poaching fails Toepfer's cash test: $5.27B, over even the unrounded $5.23B and over on a six-year spread. It also fails Wagner's stricter-condition test, which I keep standing. Both are binding soft vetoes.
- + A350 Re-engine + poaching fails both: $6.87B, and the stricter condition.
- The only survivor is the hold plan. It is also the company default and the reference row, so no tie-break is needed.

STEP 3: OVERRIDES CONSIDERED AND DECLINED (budget unused, one left)
Poaching:
- Its margin of +1.65 / +1.66 over the best passing option clears the team's $1B bar in both columns. An override would require me to record setting aside the team's stricter condition and to override Toepfer's cash test.
- I decline, for four reasons:
  - The Board has stated a Liquidity veto, which is its own test, and I hold no override against the Board. The order would revert to the default after spending the game's only override.
  - $0.6B of the $1B falls in 2037-39, after NGSA enters service, so the recruitment reading weakens.
  - It does nothing for 2045 or 2050.
  - My supply-security bias is about our own ramp, and it is no reason to order Delay Tactics.
- The stricter condition stands, as in 2030.

A350 Re-engine:
- It clears the $1B bar in S1 only (+1.54) and is -1.21 in S2, so it is worth +$0.72-0.85B probability-weighted (breaks even at 56% S2).
- On a Qualified Majority item, the Board's override review requires staying ahead of the best passing option in the worst plausible column. It fails that, and it fails the Board's Liquidity test.
- It returns in 2045 (zero overlap, $1.0B a year) only if no 787 Re-engine is on the record.

ENGINE CODE
- Code 7 is confirmed, on Wagner's supply recommendation: CFM + GTF2 (2036) + UltraFan NB (2037). That gives 3 sources and 3 makers in 2040, 2045 and 2050, and it sits in no barred pair with fps's code 7.
- No maker is off track on the record, and the code is not changed in reaction to Boeing.
- CFM certifies first and gates EIS. UltraFan never holds EIS.

BOARD-GATE LINE (package; no Board items)
- Five pillars: pass, nothing covert.
- Toepfer: pass.
  - Liquidity: $5.07B in 2035-36, nil programme cash in 2037-39, against $5.2B (EUR 4,753m at $1.10); headroom $0.13B.
  - Downside: worst column S2, +22.88.
  - Returns: payout inside 30-50%, at the lower end if ramp cash falls short; no new debt or equity.

final.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft is in its final phase of development and remains on track for entry into service in the second half of the 2030s, on the clock we set when we prepared it. We intend to offer a choice of engines. CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce are all on the programme, and each engine will join the aircraft once its maturity and durability are proven: we will not compromise on certification. Until the new aircraft enters service, the A320neo and A350 families remain our priority, with a disciplined and controlled production ramp-up, delivery performance for our customers through the transition and continued work to secure our own supply chain, engines and critical materials first. We are funding the programme with financial discipline, within our financial flexibility and our existing shareholder return policy. We will continue to work with our industry partners for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for aerospace trade. Preparing the Airbus of the 2030s means one well-prepared programme at a time, for a stronger and more sovereign European aerospace industry.
final.rationale:
DECISION BY THE TEAM RULE
Orders: ngsa hold, engine code 7 (unchanged, confirmed in its last changeable round), rea350 hold, delay_tactics none. No Board items. Row: +23.37 (S1) / +22.88 (S2). Probability-weighted at 25-30% S2: +23.22 to +23.25. I verified the grid items and the peak-cash arithmetic myself on the brief's numbers.

FRAMING, in my order
- Five pillars: nothing covert, and both colleagues raise no flag on this plan [AX-0081, AX-0073].
- Ramp: no new programme cash or engineering load in NGSA's last two spend years [AX-0010, AX-0054].
- Airbus of the 30s: NGSA whole, with entry into service in the second half of the decade and three engine sources [AX-0020, A-0409].
- Board: this is the Board's own expected package.

STEP 1: DELETE RED-LINE AND PILLAR BREACHES
- Every cancel row: rule 7. Continuing gains $39.65B in both columns. Cancelling writes off $25.37B in 2035 and drops the enabler to 2 sources. Boeing's fps is never a ground.
- Delay Tactics 'both', in any row: rule 4 (two moves), and an integrity flag from both colleagues.
- Any 'bottleneck': Toepfer (as chair of the Internal Control Committee) and Wagner both flag integrity, because the board's move exists to delay fps, not to give us a first claim for our own ramp. A pillars failure cannot be overridden.
- Left: the hold plan, + A350 Re-engine, + poaching, and + A350 Re-engine + poaching.

STEP 2: SURVIVORS OF BOTH TESTS
- Hold plan: passes both.
  - Toepfer: $5.07B in 2035-36 against $5.2B; worst column +22.88; the net-cash bridge holds under the guardrail; no break-even crossed.
  - Wagner: no pillars flag; A320 shield holds; no crunch; NGSA ready for 2037; code 7.
- + A350 Re-engine fails Toepfer twice: peak cash of $6.67B is $1.47B over the line, and the added item is -1.21 in S2. Both are binding soft vetoes. Wagner passes it at the limit but flags 2045 as the better fit.
- + poaching fails Toepfer's cash test: $5.27B, over even the unrounded $5.23B and over on a six-year spread. It also fails Wagner's stricter-condition test, which I keep standing. Both are binding soft vetoes.
- + A350 Re-engine + poaching fails both: $6.87B, and the stricter condition.
- The only survivor is the hold plan. It is also the company default and the reference row, so no tie-break is needed.

STEP 3: OVERRIDES CONSIDERED AND DECLINED (budget unused, one left)
Poaching:
- Its margin of +1.65 / +1.66 over the best passing option clears the team's $1B bar in both columns. An override would require me to record setting aside the team's stricter condition and to override Toepfer's cash test.
- I decline, for four reasons:
  - The Board has stated a Liquidity veto, which is its own test, and I hold no override against the Board. The order would revert to the default after spending the game's only override.
  - $0.6B of the $1B falls in 2037-39, after NGSA enters service, so the recruitment reading weakens.
  - It does nothing for 2045 or 2050.
  - My supply-security bias is about our own ramp, and it is no reason to order Delay Tactics.
- The stricter condition stands, as in 2030.

A350 Re-engine:
- It clears the $1B bar in S1 only (+1.54) and is -1.21 in S2, so it is worth +$0.72-0.85B probability-weighted (breaks even at 56% S2).
- On a Qualified Majority item, the Board's override review requires staying ahead of the best passing option in the worst plausible column. It fails that, and it fails the Board's Liquidity test.
- It returns in 2045 (zero overlap, $1.0B a year) only if no 787 Re-engine is on the record.

ENGINE CODE
- Code 7 is confirmed, on Wagner's supply recommendation: CFM + GTF2 (2036) + UltraFan NB (2037). That gives 3 sources and 3 makers in 2040, 2045 and 2050, and it sits in no barred pair with fps's code 7.
- No maker is off track on the record, and the code is not changed in reaction to Boeing.
- CFM certifies first and gates EIS. UltraFan never holds EIS.

BOARD-GATE LINE (package; no Board items)
- Five pillars: pass, nothing covert.
- Toepfer: pass.
  - Liquidity: $5.07B in 2035-36, nil programme cash in 2037-39, against $5.2B (EUR 4,753m at $1.10); headroom $0.13B.
  - Downside: worst column S2, +22.88.
  - Returns: payout inside 30-50%, at the lower end if ramp cash falls short; no new debt or equity.
  - The $35.52B charge at the 2037 EIS is reported beside EBIT Adjusted.
  - No break-even crossed ($35.52B < $36.4B; EUR 4,753m > EUR 4.61bn; $1.10 > $1.068).
- Wagner: pass. No quality event, no supply crunch, A320 shield held, NGSA ready for 2037, and the three-engine load is reported to the safety review.
- Grid: +23.37 / +22.88. Items held at default, with their values against hold: A350 Re-engine +1.54 / -1.21; one Delay Tactics move +1.65 / +1.66; both +1.18 / +1.19; cancel -39.65 / -39.65.

GAP TO THE BEST GRID PLAN
The best grid plan in S1 is $3.19B above the default. The gap is recorded, not paid for: every route to it fails cash, integrity or the stricter condition, and the Board vetoes each piece.

frame.question:
What game are we playing, and how do we win? [CX-0467]

The selections are made. Both new narrowbodies launched in 2030, and both chose all three engine makers (code 7). NGSA enters service in 2037 and fps in 2040. Two rival new narrowbody engines have launched and been selected on both aircraft. So the game is no longer whether we get on the next aircraft. It is the installed base on two aircraft we now share three ways ("Our major economics happen in and around the first and second" [CX-0422]), and keeping both slots through entry into service. "We don't have a birthright on that next order" [CX-0564].

Three doors close this round:
- It is the last round either airframer can change its engine code. Both enter service before the 2045 round.
- It is the last round we can cancel the Ducted (ready in 2036) or Embraer (counting from 2037).
- It is the last round an Open Fan launch could be ready by 2050 (2035 + 10 = 2045).

We win this round on execution, not on launches:
- get the Ducted ready with its durability earned by testing;
- keep both airframers on CFM through readiness, durability and support, not price ("we are not the low bid" [CX-0250]);
- keep RISE whole as technology until an airframer wants it as a product [CX-0469, CX-0205].

So the question for this room has two parts. Does anything on this grid pay us to move, or do we hold everything and put the work into delivery? And do we say plainly that the Open Fan leg of our objective is out of reach on our tests?

On the board's share rules it never does, because the +10 pp applies once any new narrowbody is in service. I would cost it as a slip of about $1.2B a year (about $1.5-1.6B with Embraer), slowing spend before any cancel.
- **Open Fan.** An airframer on the record that would take an Open Fan entering after 2045 (no new narrowbody in service before it), or a grid where the cheapest Open Fan row comes within $15B of the best non-RISE plan. Neither is on this grid.
- **Booking.** If the 2045 bulletin shows the codes locked at 7, I raise to S1 (-62.61). If an airframer signals a move toward sole source before the codes lock, I book that column (S2 -89.91 or S3 -78.31).
- **Safran.** Safran declines on the record to continue the Ducted or Embraer.
- **Capacity.** Once an airframer's volumes are agreed, I put a joint number on the capacity plan with Safran, and not before.
cfo.memo:
Larry, it's a hold round, and there's nothing to hide in the numbers. Hold is the best row in every column: -62.61, -89.91, -78.31. Every alternative loses $4.65B to $59.98B against it in every column, so the premium is nil whichever column you expect. Count: $0 of $2.0B, $0 of $4.0B, RISE allowance $0 of $15B.

The Ducted reread holds. A cancel gives up about $19.5-20.3B of engine value. On the board it saves $2.67B, not $0.67B, because the strain goes with it, and the row still loses $16.86-17.65B. An Embraer cancel saves nothing at all. Keep both.

Open Fan: the cheapest row is $31.37B below hold, twice the allowance. Say plainly the leg is out of reach.

Capex: no new R&D. The Ducted's last $0.67B and the strain we already carry come to about $1.0B a year against $2.5B of room. The 70% payout and the rating are whole.

What the case leaves out: a code switch costs $15.70-27.30B, and no lever here stops it. A Ducted slip past 2037 costs about $1.2B for the first year, $1.5-1.6B if Embraer waits with it. And the grid's volume falls, from 3,040 CFM engines a year to 1,270 from 2040, so we don't build for a ramp it doesn't show. Rates get planned privately with Safran, with no number until each airframer's volumes are worked.

Booking: -77, not -75, and raise when 2045 locks the codes. We've been proven wrong before.

tests.name: Turn on, turn off (my veto: dates)
tests.threshold: No ready year earlier than the board's development time: Ducted launch + 6; Open Fan launch + 10 and not before 2045; Embraer counts 7 years after launch; GEnx 3 years after launch, counting from the first Re-engine's entry or 2042. An order whose value depends on an earlier date fails (inference: my test standard applied to the board's development times).
tests.numbers: Ducted: launched 2030, ready 2036 (2030 + 6), not earlier. Its +10 pp counts from 2037, the first year a new narrowbody (NGSA) is in service. Partner Embraer: launched 2030, counts 2037 (2030 + 7), after the Ducted it needs (2036). GEnx upgrade: launched 2030, ready 2033 (2030 + 3). With no Re-engine on the record it counts from 2042: the brief's WB share goes from 42.0% to 44.8% in 2042. Open Fan: held. A 2035 launch would be ready in 2045 (2035 + 10, which is also the 2045 floor). That is not earlier than launch plus development time, so my binding date ground does not fail an Open Fan launch on its date. It fails the airframe test below. If we hold now, the next launch is 2045, ready 2055. Every row Culp tests (A to F and the excluded rows) uses these years, and no row's value rests on an earlier year. Pass.

tests.name: Test, not analysis (my veto: dates), with the public-line check (Culp's asks 1 and 8)
tests.threshold: Every date in the public statement or other moves must be one a test can back: no Open Fan entry before 2045, no ready date before launch plus development years, and no Ducted certification or entry claim beyond what testing has earned.
tests.numbers: Answer to ask 1: nothing behind 2036 goes beyond the board's development time. No Ducted turn-on, turn-off result is in the brief or in my record; my own words end in March 2024 and the CFM record in October 2025, before any Ducted engine. The 2036 ready year is in the bulletin because the game publishes engine-ready dates, not because a test earned it. Label it as the board's time. Answer to ask 8, Culp's draft line: (a) 'RISE remains our next generation, and our customers decide when' gives no date: pass. (b) 'No dates our testing hasn't earned' is my standard: pass. (c) 'Honored to be on both new aircraft' restates the public selection (code 7 on both), not a certification or entry claim: pass. (d) 'We earn that on readiness, durability and support' is a commitment, not a Ducted claim: pass while no number is attached. The line stays a pass only if the step-4 statement adds no Ducted certification or entry year, no claim that the Ducted enters service on NGSA or fps, no Open Fan or RISE flight-test year, no ramp date, and no fuel-burn, durability or time-on-wing claim for the Ducted.

tests.name: Ducted readiness: what certifying first needs, and the slip (Culp's ask 1)
tests.threshold: Under Boeing's public terms CFM is the baseline engine and certifies first, and the others follow once they show maturity and durability. Certifying first must be backed by test before the date is believed. The gates below are an inference from my LEAP practice.
tests.numbers: No Ducted test data exists in the brief or my record, so there is nothing yet to pass or fail. Gates to have in hand on test before certification: (1) the hot section turned on and turned off: reproduce hot-and-harsh distress in dust testing and remove it with the design. Those are the parts that cost LEAP time on wing in the Middle East and India [CX-0161]; the same dust testing started on RISE HPT blades in October 2025 [CX-0222]. (2) Life-limited parts at full life at entry. The public bulletin already sets that bar for another maker's engine, with severe-environment validation first, and CFM certifying first must clear at least the same bar on test. (3) Enhanced inspection of safety-critical parts in new-make shops and MRO from the first engine [CX-0010]. (4) Root cause and fixes accepted by the airframer and the regulator, as with Boeing and the FAA [CX-0003]. (5) Every gate a cross-functional call [CX-0012]. (6) Report back against the date, as with the fuel nozzle [CX-0007]. Float: ready 2036 against NGSA 2037 is 1 year; against fps 2040, 4 years. On the board, a Ducted ready in 2037 still counts from 2037. A slip past 2037 shows first as a gate that does not turn off. NGSA would then enter with two new rival engines ready (2036, 2037) while the CFM slot flies a LEAP derivative until the Ducted is ready. Ghai prices that at about $1.0-1.2B a year; that is his number, not mine. Track record: my LEAP-1B kit moved from 2025 to 1H 2026, about a year [CX-0008, CX-0210]. One year of float is no more than my own record has already used. If a gate fails, the date moves, not the test [CX-0208, CX-0603].

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Ducted (advice)
tests.threshold: Report the gap in years between the Ducted's ready year and the first new narrowbody's entry. A defensive Ducted earns +10 pp from its ready year once a new NB is in service; earlier is better, but a late date does not fail it. Not a veto ground (inference).
tests.numbers: Ducted ready 2036. NGSA enters 2037: 1 year ahead. fps enters 2040: 4 years ahead. Brief NB share on hold: 76.0% to 2036; 56.5% in 2037, 55.9% in 2038 and 55.2% in 2039; 31.7% from 2040. My check: 2037 (Boeing 39, Airbus 61): CFM 39 + 61/3 = 59.33, net of the engine moves (+10 Ducted, +5 Embraer, -5 GTF2, -10 UltraFan), over 105 = 56.5%. From 2040, a three-way split on both aircraft: 33.33 / 105 = 31.7%. Keeping the Ducted is worth +16.86 / +17.37 / +17.65 against cancel (row B), S1 / S2 / S3.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Open Fan launch rows D, E, F and the excluded rows (advice; Culp's ask 4)
tests.threshold: The Open Fan must be ready no later than the first new narrowbody's entry, or the board takes 35 pp of NB share (20 pp with Lobby). Report the gap. Not a veto ground, because the 2045 ready year is itself correct (inference).
tests.numbers: Confirmed, all three: (1) a 2035 launch is ready in 2045; (2) that is 8 years late against NGSA (2037) and 5 years late against fps (2040), so H2 binds in every column; (3) if we hold now, the next launch is 2045, ready 2055, after 2050. 'Launched and ready by 2050' is out of reach on our tests. Rows against hold, S1 / S2 / S3: D Open Fan -55.79 / -35.38 / -40.09; E Open Fan + Lobby -37.34 / -31.37 / -35.99; F Ducted cancel + Open Fan -58.46 / -35.73 / -42.76. This fails for any Open Fan launch. Culp's plan holds the Open Fan, so no order he leans to fails.

tests.name: RISE gates set in round 1, reported as the state of the technology (Culp's ask 5)
tests.threshold: The round-1 gates, to be in hand by the 2035 round: (1) ground and flight test done; (2) compact-core durability turned on and off, with the HPT dust testing closed; (3) more than 20% fuel burn shown in engine test, not analysis; (4) noise below today's LEAP. This is the state of the technology, not a product case, and not a veto ground.
tests.numbers: I report back against the promise: the record does not show these gates met. (1) Not shown. The fly demo was promised 'by the middle of this decade' [CX-0001, CX-0151] and moved to 'engine ground level and flight test this decade' [CX-0211]. No result is in the record, which ends in October 2025, or in the brief. (2) Not closed. Over 350 programme tests with an early focus on durability [CX-0216]; HPT-blade dust testing on the compact core began in October 2025 [CX-0222]; a Chief Mechanic and Architect for the open fan was named [CX-0223]. No turn-off result is on the record. (3) Not shown in engine test. 'More than 20%' is the design figure [CX-0001] and the physics case [CX-0180], not an engine-test result. (4) Shown as a capability: noise tested with Airbus showed the open fan 'has the capability to achieve lower noise than today's LEAP' [CX-0013], but not on a product engine. Count: none of the three Board gates closed; the fourth shown in part. The record is silent after October 2025. Promise no RISE date. There is no Open Fan order, so this informs the Board and blocks nothing.

tests.name: Physics
tests.threshold: Call RISE the next generation only at 20% or better. A ducted engine has 'less than half' the gain, so it is never the next generation. That it is a defensive step only is company doctrine (hard rule 3), not my words. Wording check on the public line (inference).
tests.numbers: Culp's red line is at least 20% for a next engine [CX-0217]. RISE: 'more than 20%' [CX-0001]; 'practically impossible ... without the open fan. And the reason is physics' [CX-0180]. A ducted engine: 'less than half' the gain [CX-0183]. The Ducted stands as an H3 defence, and the trigger is now on the public record: two rival NB engines are launched, ready in 2036 and 2037, and selected on both aircraft. Culp's draft calls RISE the next generation, never the Ducted, and gives no fuel-burn number. Pass. Any public RISE fuel-burn number would need an engine test, which the record does not show (RISE gate 3).

tests.name: Durability first (Culp's ask 2)
tests.threshold: No plan trades durability or time on wing for fuel burn or schedule. The brief has no durability data, so this is not applicable unless the brief or a statement makes a durability claim (inference; Culp's line applied to my seat).
tests.numbers: Answer to ask 2: I raise no safety or durability flag on the Ducted, Embraer or GEnx. The brief carries no durability or time-on-wing data, and no order trades durability for schedule. This is not a clearance: there is no Ducted test evidence either way, and I say so plainly. Condition for carrying the Ducted into service: the gates in the readiness test above, decided cross-functionally. If one does not turn off, the date moves, not the test [CX-0208, CX-0603]. Embraer rides on the same engine and carries the same gates. GEnx is a derivative on a proven architecture, ready since 2033, with no durability data either way. Yardstick for any later durability claim: field cycles against the CFM56, as with LEAP (9,882 cycles against about 17,000) [CX-0006], and the LEAP-1A kit's twofold gain matched to the CFM56 [CX-0209].

tests.name: Supply load (seat doctrine; Culp's ask 6)
tests.threshold: Two or more projects cost $2B of strain and load the same constrained suppliers: recommend against stacking unless the grid pays more than the strain (inference; my supply role is in Culp's words only).
tests.numbers: Hold adds no project. The Ducted, Embraer and GEnx already run, and the $2B strain is in the hold row (-2.00 of the -62.61). No evidence in my record on running the supply chain: following doctrine (the strain rule) and Culp's data [CX-0613]. Board volumes for the joint capacity plan (hold, S1): CFM NB engines 3,040 a year to 2036; 2,260 (2037), 2,235 (2038), 2,210 (2039); 1,270 a year from 2040, out of a 4,000-engine market. WB: 143 a year, 152 from 2042. On the board, CFM's unit load falls. The strain is the mix: a new engine's hot-section and safety-critical parts entering production in 2036-37 on the same base that carries the LEAP rate, the GE9X ramp and the durability kits, behind 9 suppliers at 15 sites with 80% of past shortages [CX-0613]. 'Support both rates' is at most today's 3,040 a year on the board, or 4,000 if one maker held both full slots. There is no supplier field data in the brief, so I give no supply 'no', and no supply 'yes' on test either. The capacity commitment is joint with Safran and private, with no number in public, under Culp's haircut. OE comes before spares [CX-0529], and enhanced inspection runs in new-make shops [CX-0010]. An Open Fan launch would stack a fourth programme ($8B) on the same suppliers, and the grid does not pay it.

tests.name: Fix, don't redesign
tests.threshold: On the widebody, prefer the GEnx upgrade on a proven architecture over a new engine; on the narrowbody, keep RISE technology flowing into LEAP upgrades while RISE matures. This does not argue against the Open Fan as the next generation (inference).
tests.numbers: The hold keeps the GEnx upgrade on the GE90/GEnx architecture [CX-0169]. It counts from 2042. LEAP keeps taking RISE technology while RISE matures [CX-0162], and a LEAP derivative is CFM's place on both aircraft if the Ducted slips (CFM is never dropped). If a Ducted test fails, fix the part rather than redesign the engine or cancel it [CX-0005].

tests.name: Safety call
tests.threshold: If a problem in the brief or an order touches safety or durability, it needs a cross-functional team, not one person.
tests.numbers: No problem in the brief touches safety. The Ducted moves into certification and production qualification in 2036-37, so durability is in play. Culp's other move (1) brings the readiness and durability review to the full Board before NGSA's 2037 entry, on turn-on, turn-off evidence, with every design and test gate a cross-functional call. Production qualification of safety-critical parts goes under the same rule. 'No single person can make a safety decision.'

tests.name: Partner Embraer date (Culp's ask 3)
tests.threshold: Embraer counts 7 years after launch and needs a new CFM engine. Its count year must not come before that engine's ready year (inference).
tests.numbers: Confirmed: launched 2030, counts 2037 (2030 + 7), on the Ducted ready in 2036. +5 pp NB from 2037. A cancel is -4.65 / -6.02 / -5.44 against hold. No engineering evidence on Embraer in my record: following Culp and doctrine. State no Embraer date in public.

tests.name: GEnx date (Culp's ask 7)
tests.threshold: GEnx counts 3 years after launch, and not before the first Re-engine's entry (2042 if neither airframer re-engines) (inference).
tests.numbers: Launched 2030, ready 2033. It counts from 2042, since no Re-engine is on the record; the brief has WB at 42.0%, then 44.8% from 2042. If a 787 or A350 Re-engine launched this round, it would enter in 2040 (launch + 5) and GEnx would count from then. The upgrade has been ready since 2033, so there is no date issue either way. GE alone.

vetoes.plan: open_fan: launch, alone or with Lobby, an Embraer cancel or a Ducted cancel (rows D, E, F and the excluded rows)
vetoes.ground: Advice only, not a date veto. The 2045 ready year is launch + 10 and also the 2045 floor, so my binding date ground does not fail it. It fails ready-no-later-than-the-airframe: 8 years late against NGSA (2037) and 5 years late against fps (2040), losing 35 pp of NB share (20 pp with Lobby). Against hold, S1 / S2 / S3: D -55.79 / -35.38 / -40.09; E -37.34 / -31.37 / -35.99. And no RISE gate stands closed on the record: no flight test, no compact-core turn-off and no 20% in engine test. A RISE product would have nothing on test behind it.

vetoes.plan: ducted: cancel (row B, or the swap in row F), with partner_embraer falling with it
vetoes.ground: Advice only. Cancels are not my veto ground, and my record is silent on cancelling: following Culp, doctrine and the Board's cancellation test. On dates, the Ducted is the only new CFM engine that can be ready for either entry (2036, against 2037 and 2040). Cancelled, the CFM slot flies a LEAP derivative beside two new rival engines ready in 2036 and 2037. Against hold: -16.86 / -17.37 / -17.65. If a test failure comes, the answer is to fix the part, not to cancel the engine: 'We failed twice. We got it done.'

vetoes.plan: Pre-notice for step 4, not an objection to Culp's lean: a public statement or other move that gives a Ducted certification or entry-into-service year, claims the Ducted enters service on NGSA or fps, gives an Open Fan or RISE flight-test or entry year or a capacity ramp date, or makes a fuel-burn, durability or time-on-wing claim for the Ducted
vetoes.ground: Binding ground 2 (a public date or claim no real test backs). 2036 is the board's development time, published by the game, not a turn-on, turn-off result. No RISE flight test or engine-test fuel burn is on the record, and no supplier field data backs a ramp date. Nothing is vetoed now. If the step-4 statement carries such a date, I veto it then, and the veto binds unless Culp answers with test evidence. Note: my veto right over programme dates is an inference. My words date from 2024, when I was VP of Engineering, and concern believing durability-fix results; the team rule and the GM read them as a binding date test.

ops.would_change_mind_if: Test or field data only, never analysis. (1) A Ducted or core test showing a failure not yet turned off, or a gate slipping 2036 past the one-year float to 2037. I would then raise a durability flag, and the date moves for a cross-functional answer. I would still argue to fix the part, not cancel the engine. (2) Supplier field data: shortages concentrating again in the 9 suppliers at 15 sites, or LEAP OE deliveries missing on them. I would then give a supply 'no' to any added work and cut the private capacity commitment. (3) A durability finding in the brief, such as a maturity slip on the Ducted or the LEAP fleet, which would bring a flag. (4) On RISE: the flight test done, the compact core turned on and off and more than 20% shown in engine test would change the state of the technology. They would not change this round's Open Fan call. NGSA (2037) and fps (2040) both enter service before a 2045 Open Fan, so the gap is the airframe, not the test. (5) A Re-engine on the record would move the GEnx count year to its entry (2040 for a 2035 launch). I would recheck that date, not the order.
ops.memo:
Larry, testing, not analysis.

Dates. Every order passes. Ducted: 2030 plus 6 is 2036, one year of float to NGSA's 2037 entry, four to fps in 2040. Embraer counts 2037, after the engine it rides on. GEnx ready since 2033, counts 2042. But 2036 is the board's development time. No Ducted engine has been turned on and turned off. Label it that way.

Certifying first means the hot section turned on and turned off in hot-and-harsh dust testing, life-limited parts at full life, enhanced inspection from the first engine, and fixes the airframer and regulator accept. My LEAP-1B kit came a year after I said. One year of float is exactly that. If a gate fails, the date moves, not the test.

Flag. None: no failure is in front of me. That is not a clearance. Every gate is cross-functional; the review goes to the full Board before 2037.

Open Fan. Launched now, ready 2045: eight years late against 2037, five against 2040. Hold now, and the next launch is ready in 2055. 'Ready by 2050' is out of reach. RISE gates on the record: flight test not shown; dust testing started, not closed; 20% is physics and design, not engine test; lower noise than LEAP shown with Airbus. Technology, not a product.

Supply. No field data: following doctrine. Our NB units fall from 3,040 to 1,270; the load is a new-engine ramp on the same nine suppliers. No supply 'no', no number in public.

Hold everything. No veto.

other_moves.move: Ducted readiness and durability review at the full Board before NGSA's 2037 entry into service
Joint CFM capacity plan with Safran for both airframers' rates
other_moves.detail:
It is built privately through CFM governance on Ali's supply data: the 9 suppliers at 15 sites behind 80% of past shortages [CX-0613]. OE comes before spares [CX-0529]. No number goes to an airframer or the public until that airframer's volumes are agreed [CX-0944], and nothing is said without Safran [CX-0184].
- The grid's CFM narrowbody volume falls: 3,040 a year to 2036, 2,260 in 2037 and 1,270 from 2040 in S1. So we build no facilities for a ramp the board doesn't show, and capex stays inside 2-3% of revenue.
- The load is the mix, not the count: a new engine's hot-section and safety-critical parts entering production in 2036-37 beside the LEAP rate, the GE9X ramp and the durability kits.
- I take a quarter to half off any ramp promise, mine included [CX-0590, CX-0592].

other_moves.move: Answer Boeing's engine competition and Airbus's risk-sharing invitation through CFM governance
other_moves.detail:
We take part in both on standard terms, priced jointly with Safran, and keep it private [CX-0184, CX-0586].
- Development is cost-plus or risk-share, never fixed price.
- No launch-era pricing [CX-0930], and no risk-share contribution, entry fee or free-engine term that works as a price concession (Ghai's terms test).
- Risk-share is modelled conservatively.
We keep the baseline, certify-first position Boeing has offered by being ready and durable, not by price: 'we are not the low bid' [CX-0250]. We refuse no airframer and lock none out (H1) [CX-0587].

other_moves.move: Keep RISE funded as technology, and report its gates as the state of the technology
CFM parity record for a hold
other_moves.detail: This round there is no new CFM narrowbody order. Continuing the Ducted and Embraer stays within joint practice: both airframers selected CFM, and the partners split the aftermarket equally [CX-0219, CX-0184]. Safran cannot be consulted in this game, so this record asserts no Safran position. GEnx is GE alone.

decision.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That doesn't change this year.

Let me tell you what we know and what we don't. Both new single-aisle aircraft have launched, and both customers chose to put CFM on them alongside others. We're honored by that. We also know we don't have a birthright on any of it. We keep a place on an airplane the same way we earned it: readiness, durability and support, one customer and one engine at a time. CFM is a 50-50 partnership with our partner, and we do this work together.

Our ducted engine is in its last year of development. It goes into service when testing says it's ready, and not a day before. Durability doesn't get traded for schedule. Our work with Embraer continues. There are no new programmes from us this year. We'll fund what we have within our capital allocation framework and keep the balance sheet where it is.

RISE remains our next generation. We're all in on the open fan technology, and it stays funded as technology. It's really not for us to say when that architecture enters service. Our customers decide when. The new aircraft come first, and we won't ask anyone to wait.

Here's what we don't know: how fast our customers will want to go once they're flying, and how those fleets will split. We won't give you dates or numbers our testing and our customers haven't earned. Commercial matters we work privately, with our customers and with our partner. You'll ask about competition. I won't speak to that. We judge ourselves on our own execution. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: HOLD EVERYTHING. All five fields are at hold. That is the default, so no order is a Board item.

WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN [CX-0467]
The selections are made. NGSA (2037) and fps (2040) both chose code 7, and two rival NB engines are selected on both. The game now is the installed base on two aircraft we share three ways [CX-0422]. This is the last round either airframer can change its code. Nothing on this grid defends against a switch, and S2 and S3 cost $27.30B and $15.70B against S1. So we win on execution, not launches:
- the Ducted ready on test, with durability earned;
- both customers kept on readiness, durability and support, not price [CX-0250];
- RISE kept whole as technology.
We have no birthright [CX-0564].

GRID AGAINST DO NOTHING (hold = Do Nothing = default)
Hold is the best plan in every column: S1 -62.61, S2 -89.91, S3 -78.31.
- Expected column (S1): best plan hold, 0.00 against Do Nothing.
- Worst column (S2): best plan hold, 0.00.
Every alternative loses in every column (S1 / S2 / S3 against hold):
- Embraer cancel: -4.65 / -6.02 / -5.44.
- Ducted cancel, with Embraer falling with it: -16.86 / -17.37 / -17.65.
- Open Fan: -55.79 / -35.38 / -40.09.
- Open Fan + Lobby: -37.34 / -31.37 / -35.99.
- Ducted cancel + Open Fan: -58.46 / -35.73 / -42.76.
Weighted on my weights (.50 / .25 / .25), hold is -73.36:
- Ducted cancel -17.19;
- Embraer cancel -5.19;
- Open Fan -46.76;
- Open Fan + Lobby -35.51.
No weighting changes the ranking. Ghai's weights (.60 / .20 / .20) and equal weights give the same answer.

TESTS
- Additive and paid for the risk: no move off hold beats hold in any column.
- Low case first: S1 is the record, and I book well below it.
- H2, the airframer sets the date: a 2035 Open Fan is ready in 2045. That is eight years after NGSA's entry and five after fps's, so it waits in every column.
- H3, the Ducted only as a defence: the trigger is now on the public record. Two rival NB engines are launched and selected on both aircraft, so keeping the Ducted is the defence the rule calls for.
- Cancel doctrine: the trigger is not met. Both airframes would fly the engine, and the threat is present.
- My 20% line binds RISE, not the Ducted. The Ducted gets 'less than half' the gain [CX-0183] and stands only under H3. The public line never calls it the next generation.
- Durability line [CX-0208]: no order trades durability for schedule. The readiness review is how I enforce that.
- Tie-break: not needed. No alternative is within $1B of hold, and the smallest gap is $4.65B.

DUCTED REREAD (round-1 commitment)
A cancel writes off $4B x 5/6 = $3.33B and saves $0.67B of R&D. Ghai's correction: on the board, the saving is $2.67B including the $2B strain released. The row still loses $16.86-17.65B, because it gives up about $19.6-20.3B of engine value. In S1 the NB share in 2037 would fall from 56.5% to 44.3%. Keep it. Once it is ready in 2036 it can no longer be cancelled, so this hold locks it in. If a test gate fails, we fix the part, not cancel the engine [CX-0005].

OPEN FAN AND THE RISE ALLOWANCE
My installed-base lens pulls hardest here [CX-0555], because this is the last round 'ready by 2050' can be met. But the cheapest row, Open Fan + Lobby, is $31.37B to $37.34B below hold ($35.51B weighted), more than twice the $15B allowance. Ali reports none of the three Board RISE gates closed on the record. So I keep RISE as technology, with no cancel (H5) and no program dividend [CX-0174]. Lobby does nothing without a live Open Fan.

SAFRAN GATE (H7)

final.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That doesn't change this year.

Let me tell you what we know and what we don't. Both new single-aisle aircraft have launched, and both customers chose to put CFM on them alongside others. We're honored by that. We also know we don't have a birthright on any of it. We keep a place on an airplane the same way we earned it: readiness, durability and support, one customer and one engine at a time. CFM is a 50-50 partnership with our partner, and we do this work together.

Our ducted engine is in its last year of development. It goes into service when testing says it's ready, and not a day before. Durability doesn't get traded for schedule. Our work with Embraer continues. There are no new programmes from us this year. We'll fund what we have within our capital allocation framework and keep the balance sheet where it is.

RISE remains our next generation. We're all in on the open fan technology, and it stays funded as technology. It's really not for us to say when that architecture enters service. Our customers decide when. The new aircraft come first, and we won't ask anyone to wait.

Here's what we don't know: how fast our customers will want to go once they're flying, and how those fleets will split. We won't give you dates or numbers our testing and our customers haven't earned. Commercial matters we work privately, with our customers and with our partner. You'll ask about competition. I won't speak to that. We judge ourselves on our own execution. It's that simple, ain't that hard.

frame.question:
Control what you can control. Both new narrowbodies now carry code 7. NGSA and fps have each selected CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce, and our 2030 `launch_if_selected` fired. GTF2 is live and will be ready in 2036, ahead of both entries into service on the record. This is the last round in which GTF2 can be cancelled: it is ready in 2036, and after that its bill is sunk. On the rules it is also the last round in which either airframer can change its code before entry into service, since the next round is 2045 (inference). So I put three questions to the ExCo.

(1) Do we keep GTF2 whole? On the grid, cancel loses in every column, and it would throw away two selections our customers put on the record.

(2) Both live airframes now carry a Rolls-Royce code, so do we put a standing, public Joint Venture commitment on the record, and on what terms? Risk and investment are shared. The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay ours.

(3) What protects the code 7 selections? They are worth more than any order on this grid: losing NGSA (S1 to S2) swings 21.32, and losing fps (S1 to S3) swings 11.81. The lever is durability validated before entry into service, not price, and the fleet still comes first.

My usual questions apply. Is the demand visible? It is on the record. Do the business model, timing and volume work? Is durability mature at entry into service? Is this a responsible bet with a responsible payback? Is the dividend safe?

frame.initial_lean:
LEAN: `gtf2_solo: hold`, `jv_with_rr: commit` (row A). Premium: $0 this round.

GTF2: hold. Two airframers have put us on the record, so the demand is visible [PX-0109]. GTF2 is ready before both entries into service, and cancel trails hold by 11.47 to 32.79 in every column. Cancelling now would also throw away the credibility objective.

Joint Venture: commit. My round-1 trigger is met: both live airframes carry code 7, which includes Rolls-Royce.
- The grid makes it weakly dominant: 0 / 0 / 0 / +5.51 against hold, +0.83 at my prior. It costs no new R&D while GTF2 is live.
- I have no record of my own on a Rolls-Royce Joint Venture (Low). This is doctrine plus Neil's cash test and Shane's technical test. The company has run Joint Ventures to spread risk and investment [P-1233][P-1676], and I call our GTF partnerships 'critical' [PX-0038].
- The lean holds only on four conditions:
  - the gear, core and GTF2 technology stay P&W modules;
  - Shane passes it on durability and parts, so GTF2's 2036 date and team are untouched and nothing is drawn from the fleet;
  - Neil confirms a $0 fold write-off and raises no veto;
  - a 2045 hold-or-withdraw re-test is written in.
- If any condition fails, I fall back to hold/hold (B), the Board's own alternative. I would declare the PV given up (5.51 × pS4) as the cost of a red line, and I have no override.

Bias check:
- Architecture loyalty would keep me on GTF2 alone. The grid says the commit never costs the GTF2 anything, so loyalty does not get to cost PV.
- Optimism on dates: I state no EIS for any airframer and no ready year before 2036. One year of margin on NGSA is thin, and my own dates have slipped by between a quarter and two years.

Expected column: S1, rivals hold. Airbus has said 'a choice of engines', Boeing wants two or three sources, and Rolls-Royce waits for our commitment.

Premium ledger: Board item 0 (the commit never trails hold); doctrine 0; objective 0. The round-1 doctrine premium of $0.26B is carried separately.

PROPOSED DISCLOSURE (public):
"Bad news first. GTF2 will be ready in 2036 and no earlier, and our dates have slipped before. So we are not compressing a single test to hold that date. Before GTF2 enters service on NGSA or fps it has to clear two gates: durability validated in severe-environment testing, and every life-limited part at full life. If anything has to give, the date moves, not the testing. The fleet still comes first. We keep inserting the Hot Section durability kit across the GTF fleet, and we review the pacing parts every week so that no new programme takes parts or engineers from that work. We control what we can control. Airbus has invited us to join its new single-aisle as a risk-sharing partner, and we accept on standard commercial terms: no launch-style discount, no concession, no free upgrade. Today Pratt & Whitney puts on the record its commitment to a Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce on the next narrowbody engine. It forms only when Rolls-Royce also commits, and until then nothing has formed. It shares risk and investment; it does not share technology. The gear and the core stay Pratt & Whitney's, and GTF2's date and team do not change. We will offer only what can be ready by an airframe's entry into service, and we will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates or rates. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks."

If Shane or Neil strikes the commit, the Joint Venture paragraph comes out and the rest stands.

ops.proposal:
PROPOSAL (Eddy, operating seat; Calio decides). gtf2_solo: hold. jv_with_rr: commit, on four technical conditions.

- gtf2_solo: hold. GTF2 has been live since the 2030 trigger and is ready in 2036. NGSA (EIS 2037) and fps (EIS 2040) both carry code 7, so it serves two live airframes that include P&W. Hold row, S1-S4: +3.37 / -17.95 / -8.44 / +3.37. My record says nothing on cancelling. Hold is the default, and company doctrine on a slip is "add testing, do not cancel" (profile §5 row 10). Cancel is flagged to Mitchill and Calio below.
- jv_with_rr: commit. My trigger is met: a live airframe's code includes Rolls-Royce (code 7 on both). The technical tests pass on the board. If it forms in 2035 (S4), the engine is GTF2 by the fold, ready 2036. Item against hold: 0 / 0 / 0 / +5.51 (brief §3, Mitchill's number). It adds no engineering until it forms. My record has no evidence on a Joint Venture, so this is seat and company doctrine [P-1233][P-1240][P-1875]. Conditions:
  (a) The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay P&W modules, with P&W keeping design authority [P-1233]. Risk and investment are shared as with our collaboration partners [P-1714][P-1744].
  (b) GTF2's configuration is frozen through entry into service. No UltraFan NB content goes into GTF2 before EIS. Merged content comes later as a derivative with its own durability programme.
  (c) Integration is staffed outside the fleet durability team and GTF2 validation.
  (d) The 2045 hold-or-withdraw re-test is written in.
  If (b) or (c) fails, I invoke ground 1 or ground 2. A failure of (a) is a company red line, not my ground, and I would flag it at the veto check.

ANSWERS TO CALIO'S ASKS
1. Orders: as above.
2. GTF2 readiness: ready 2036 (launch 2030 + 6). Margin is 1 year to NGSA 2037 and 4 years to fps 2040.
- Severe-environment validation: I can't give a status. The board carries no test results, and I won't call them done [PX-0112].
- The gates are the Advantage's: endurance testing at representative severe conditions [PX-0128], more than double the original programme's [P-0779], and every LLP at full life at EIS [P-0785].
- On the board there is no slip. The real margin is thinner. The Advantage aimed at mid-2024 and certified in 2025, about a year late. The company prior for a derivative is +1.5 to 2 years (profile §3).
- So 1 year of slip uses up the NGSA margin, and slipping at the prior puts GTF2 at about 2037.5-2038, after NGSA's EIS. fps absorbs it.
- What gives first is the date, and with it our slot at NGSA's entry, not the testing. If that happens we follow on NGSA as Boeing already sequences us.
3. Fleet:
- No 2035 AOG count and no pacing-parts count. I cannot give them. My data stop at 10% AOG in June 2023 [PX-0120], about 350 AOG on average through 2026 with a 600-650 peak [PX-0300][P-1039], and about 30 pacing parts [PX-0123].
- Hot Section kit progress in 2035 is not in evidence. From 2026 the kit carries 90-95% of the Advantage's gains, and it is charged [P-1363][P-1813].
- The 2036-37 GTF2 ramp is the real draw. Our last escape came from ramp capacity [P-1040][P-1062]. So: ring-fence it from the AOG recovery and kit insertion, review pacing parts weekly [PX-0131], and qualify new castings, forgings and powder-metal capacity before it ships parts (contain first, inference) [PX-0121].
4. Joint Venture readiness:
- If it forms in 2035 (S4), it is ready in 2036 through the GTF2 fold. UltraFan NB (2037) also folds, and the earlier date counts. Against 2037 and 2040: pass.
- If it forms in 2045, both airframes are already in service. GTF2 would be about 8 years into service on NGSA and 5 on fps, possibly mid-campaign (prior: 2-3 retrofit campaigns in years 1-5; about 2 years each [P-0895]).
- "One engine" is then a fiction: two certified, fielded engine types and two support chains [P-1875].
- We would share risk on UltraFan NB durability that we never validated. Partners pay their share of defects [P-1563].
- For the 2045 re-test: technical due diligence on RR fleet data, and no draw on GTF2 fleet support.
5. Technical conditions: yes, by module ownership. This is the collaboration model in which P&W is principal and keeps 51-57% [P-1744][P-1747]. Design teams mirror the architecture, so each module's owner keeps that module's team [P-1240]. In 2035 the fold makes one engine (GTF2), with UltraFan NB stopped as a separate product [P-1875]. Staffing outside the fleet and validation teams is my condition. RR claims favourable geared IP [P-2004]: the gear is where IP would cross, so P&W keeps the gear team and data.
6. Engineering load: one programme. GTF2 validation, the ramp and any fold make one engine. Integration is an overlay. The peak is 2035-37. Advice only; the board has no strain charge.
7. Evidence for the airframers:
- For Airbus before 2037: severe-environment endurance results, full-life LLP certification, test-engine teardown findings (inference), and the GTF fleet's kit record.
- For Boeing 2036-40: all of that, plus NGSA field data if NGSA enters on time. The benchmark is about 1M fleet hours to surface issues [P-0847], so that gives about one fix campaign before fps (inference).
- Data on a cadence, not time-on-wing claims. Durability, not price, protects code 7.
8. Vetoes:
- gtf2_solo hold: passes both grounds.
- cancel: neither of my grounds; I propose hold.
- jv_with_rr commit: passes both grounds on conditions (b) and (c).
- Option D: neither of my grounds. Its Joint Venture engine is ready 2037 through the UltraFan fold, zero margin to NGSA (advice).
- Disclosure draft: passes. 2036 and no earlier, with gates rather than claims.
