decision.public_statement:
Bad news first. GTF2 has not yet earned its durability record, and our dates have slipped before. GTF2 is in development for NGSA and fps. It will be ready in 2036 and no earlier, and we are not compressing a single test to hold that date. Before it enters service it has to clear two gates: durability validated in severe-environment testing, and every life-limited part at full life. Those are gates, not claims. If anything has to give, the date moves, not the testing.

The fleet still comes first. We keep inserting the Hot Section durability kit across the GTF fleet, and we review the pacing parts every week so that neither the GTF2 ramp nor any Joint Venture work takes parts or engineers from that work. We control what we can control.

Airbus has invited us onto its new single-aisle as a risk-sharing partner. We accept on standard commercial terms: we carry our own engine's development, and there is no launch-style discount, no concession and no free upgrade. On fps we follow in sequence once we show maturity and durability. That is the right test, and we will meet it with test data, not with price.

Today Pratt & Whitney puts on the record its commitment to a Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce on the next narrowbody engine. It forms only if and when Rolls-Royce also commits, and until then nothing has formed. It shares risk and investment, not technology. The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay Pratt & Whitney's, and GTF2's configuration, date and team do not change.

We will offer only what can be ready by an airframe's entry into service, and we will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates or rates. Those are theirs to announce. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: `gtf2_solo: hold`, `jv_with_rr: commit` (row 'GTF2: hold + commit to JV': +3.37 / -17.95 / -8.44 / +8.88). It is Eddy's proposal and Mitchill's recommendation, and both pass every veto. overrides is empty.

1. Constraint first [PX-0035][PX-0073].
- On the board GTF2 is ready in 2036: one year before NGSA's 2037 EIS and four before fps's 2040. Eddy's binding readiness test passes on both.
- Bad news first: the real margin is thinner than the board's. The Advantage slipped about a year, and the company prior for a derivative is +1.5 to 2 years, which would land GTF2 around 2037.5-2038, after NGSA's EIS. My own dates have slipped by one quarter to two years [PX-0017][PX-0098][PX-0104].
- So I book nothing on the date. The two gates (severe-environment validation, full-life LLPs at EIS) are gates, not claims, and the date moves, not the testing. Mitchill prices a slip past 2037 at up to 21.32 (the S2 outcome). That is a red-line cost, not traded.
- The Joint Venture must not touch GTF2's configuration, team or date (Eddy's conditions b and c).
- Fleet first [PX-0080]: the 2036-37 ramp is the real draw, so it is ring-fenced under the weekly pacing-parts review, and new capacity is qualified before it ships.

2. GTF2: hold.
- The demand is visible: code 7 on both live airframes, on the record [PX-0109].
- Cancel trails hold in every column: -32.79 / -11.47 / -20.98 / -32.79. That is -29.26 at my weights and -29.05 at Mitchill's. It would write off $1.67B to save $0.33B and throw away two selections.
- I do not harvest a programme its customers chose. This is inference from [PX-0064][P-1342]: we reset what has stopped working, and this has not.
- Mitchill confirms hold carries a selected engine, so ground 2 does not reach it.
- From 2036 GTF2's $2B is sunk and the cancel option lapses.

3. Joint Venture: commit.
- My round-1 trigger is met: code 7 on both live airframes includes Rolls-Royce.
- The item against hold is 0 / 0 / 0 / +5.51, never negative. That is +0.55 at my weights, +0.44 at Mitchill's and +1.38 at equal weights.
- It needs $0 of new cash: GTF2's $2B equals our share, so the fold write-off is $0 (Mitchill). It beats a buyback, which is about $0 NPV at the 10% WACC.
- I have no record of my own on a Rolls-Royce Joint Venture (Low). This is company doctrine (profile.md §6, dashboard_game.md §5; [P-1233][P-1676]) plus Mitchill's cash test and Eddy's technical test as my evidence. I call our GTF partnerships 'critical' [PX-0038].
- Terms: risk and investment shared, never the gear, core or GTF2 technology, which stay P&W modules under P&W design authority.
- Eddy's flag that Rolls-Royce claims favourable geared IP is rebutted in the terms: P&W keeps the gear team and data. No core-technology red-line flag is left standing.
- Architecture loyalty would have kept me on GTF2 alone. The grid says the commit costs GTF2 nothing, so loyalty does not get to cost PV.

4. Veto check.
- Mitchill, ground by ground:
  - ground 1 (dividend or debt): no new R&D; GTF2 cost $0.33B a year, 5.6% of the ~$6B envelope; dividend covered; debt on its pre-ASR path; no envelope stretch.
  - ground 2 (unselected engine): pass.
  - ground 3 (aggressive terms): standard terms in the Airbus and Boeing answers, no buy-in payment.
  - ground 4 (booking upside): $0 booked on the commit, and nothing is presented as formed.
- His two conditional binding vetoes are respected in the statement and other moves:
  - ground 4: Rolls-Royce's commitment and the formation are not presented as done; the +5.51 is not announced; durability is written as gates.
  - ground 3: no concession, discount, fee or fixed-price development.
- Eddy: both grounds pass on the orders as proposed. His standing conditions (configuration freeze; staffing outside the fleet and validation teams) are written into other moves, so neither is invoked.

5. Red lines.
- No new engine without a committed airframer: GTF2 fired on code 7 selections.
- Shared-source relief on code 7 (NGSA and fps) is declared again, as in round 1. On NGSA it is also franchise defence (inference: [PX-0058][P-1292]).
- No core technology to the Joint Venture [P-1233].
- The dividend never funds an engine.
- Value, not share [PX-0055][PX-0100].
- No widebody [PX-0027].
- No airframer dates or rates [PX-0062].

6. Premium: $0 this round.
- No Board item trails hold, and neither a doctrine nor an objective premium is needed.
- Round-1 doctrine premium: $0.26B, reported separately. The cumulative ledger is $0.26B inside the $1B cap.

7. Objective.
- Restore credibility is met (on the board) in every column: on NGSA and fps in S1/S4, fps in S2, NGSA in S3. It holds only while GTF2 is ready by EIS. We do not claim it in public.
- Capitalise is met in S1 and S4 (+3.37 / +8.88) and fails in S2 and S3 in every row. No order moves those columns; only durability data the airframers believe does.

8. Expected column: S1, rivals hold.
- Airbus keeps 'a choice of engines', Boeing wants two or three sources, and Rolls-Royce waits for our commitment to be on the record.
- I lowered S4 from 0.15 to 0.10 on Mitchill's point that orders are sealed and simultaneous, and raised S2 to 0.11 on GTF reputation risk.
- Expected PV +0.39 against hold's -0.16.

What would change my mind:
- Joint Venture terms needing P&W cash beyond GTF2's $2B: back through the gate.
- A slip or parts shortfall that Eddy reports: hold/hold, and the date moves.
- In 2045, the written re-test.

final.public_statement:
Bad news first. GTF2 has not yet earned its durability record, and our dates have slipped before. GTF2 is in development for NGSA and fps. It will be ready in 2036 and no earlier, and we are not compressing a single test to hold that date. Before it enters service it has to clear two gates: durability validated in severe-environment testing, and every life-limited part at full life. Those are gates, not claims. If anything has to give, the date moves, not the testing.

The fleet still comes first. We keep inserting the Hot Section durability kit across the GTF fleet, and we review the pacing parts every week so that neither the GTF2 ramp nor any Joint Venture work takes parts or engineers from that work. We control what we can control.

Airbus has invited us onto its new single-aisle as a risk-sharing partner. We accept on standard commercial terms: we carry our own engine's development, and there is no launch-style discount, no concession and no free upgrade. On fps we follow in sequence once we show maturity and durability. That is the right test, and we will meet it with test data, not with price.

Today Pratt & Whitney puts on the record its commitment to a Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce on the next narrowbody engine. It forms only if and when Rolls-Royce also commits, and until then nothing has formed. It shares risk and investment, not technology. The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay Pratt & Whitney's, and GTF2's configuration, date and team do not change.

We will offer only what can be ready by an airframe's entry into service, and we will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates or rates. Those are theirs to announce. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks.
final.rationale:
DECISION: `gtf2_solo: hold`, `jv_with_rr: commit` (row 'GTF2: hold + commit to JV': +3.37 / -17.95 / -8.44 / +8.88). It is Eddy's proposal and Mitchill's recommendation, and both pass every veto. overrides is empty.

1. Constraint first [PX-0035][PX-0073].
- On the board GTF2 is ready in 2036: one year before NGSA's 2037 EIS and four before fps's 2040. Eddy's binding readiness test passes on both.
- Bad news first: the real margin is thinner than the board's. The Advantage slipped about a year, and the company prior for a derivative is +1.5 to 2 years, which would land GTF2 around 2037.5-2038, after NGSA's EIS. My own dates have slipped by one quarter to two years [PX-0017][PX-0098][PX-0104].
- So I book nothing on the date. The two gates (severe-environment validation, full-life LLPs at EIS) are gates, not claims, and the date moves, not the testing. Mitchill prices a slip past 2037 at up to 21.32 (the S2 outcome). That is a red-line cost, not traded.
- The Joint Venture must not touch GTF2's configuration, team or date (Eddy's conditions b and c).
- Fleet first [PX-0080]: the 2036-37 ramp is the real draw, so it is ring-fenced under the weekly pacing-parts review, and new capacity is qualified before it ships.

2. GTF2: hold.
- The demand is visible: code 7 on both live airframes, on the record [PX-0109].
- Cancel trails hold in every column: -32.79 / -11.47 / -20.98 / -32.79. That is -29.26 at my weights and -29.05 at Mitchill's. It would write off $1.67B to save $0.33B and throw away two selections.
- I do not harvest a programme its customers chose. This is inference from [PX-0064][P-1342]: we reset what has stopped working, and this has not.
- Mitchill confirms hold carries a selected engine, so ground 2 does not reach it.
- From 2036 GTF2's $2B is sunk and the cancel option lapses.

3. Joint Venture: commit.
- My round-1 trigger is met: code 7 on both live airframes includes Rolls-Royce.
- The item against hold is 0 / 0 / 0 / +5.51, never negative. That is +0.55 at my weights, +0.44 at Mitchill's and +1.38 at equal weights.
- It needs $0 of new cash: GTF2's $2B equals our share, so the fold write-off is $0 (Mitchill). It beats a buyback, which is about $0 NPV at the 10% WACC.
- I have no record of my own on a Rolls-Royce Joint Venture (Low). This is company doctrine (profile.md §6, dashboard_game.md §5; [P-1233][P-1676]) plus Mitchill's cash test and Eddy's technical test as my evidence. I call our GTF partnerships 'critical' [PX-0038].
- Terms: risk and investment shared, never the gear, core or GTF2 technology, which stay P&W modules under P&W design authority.
- Eddy's flag that Rolls-Royce claims favourable geared IP is rebutted in the terms: P&W keeps the gear team and data. No core-technology red-line flag is left standing.
- Architecture loyalty would have kept me on GTF2 alone. The grid says the commit costs GTF2 nothing, so loyalty does not get to cost PV.

4. Veto check.
- Mitchill, ground by ground:
  - ground 1 (dividend or debt): no new R&D; GTF2 cost $0.33B a year, 5.6% of the ~$6B envelope; dividend covered; debt on its pre-ASR path; no envelope stretch.
  - ground 2 (unselected engine): pass.
  - ground 3 (aggressive terms): standard terms in the Airbus and Boeing answers, no buy-in payment.
  - ground 4 (booking upside): $0 booked on the commit, and nothing is presented as formed.
- His two conditional binding vetoes are respected in the statement and other moves:
  - ground 4: Rolls-Royce's commitment and the formation are not presented as done; the +5.51 is not announced; durability is written as gates.
  - ground 3: no concession, discount, fee or fixed-price development.
- Eddy: both grounds pass on the orders as proposed. His standing conditions (configuration freeze; staffing outside the fleet and validation teams) are written into other moves, so neither is invoked.

5. Red lines.
- No new engine without a committed airframer: GTF2 fired on code 7 selections.
- Shared-source relief on code 7 (NGSA and fps) is declared again, as in round 1. On NGSA it is also franchise defence (inference: [PX-0058][P-1292]).
- No core technology to the Joint Venture [P-1233].

6. Premium: $0 this round.

7. Objective.
- Restore credibility is met (on the board) in every column: on NGSA and fps in S1/S4, fps in S2, NGSA in S3. It holds only while GTF2 is ready by EIS. We do not claim it in public.

PUBLIC RECORD (bulletin, round 2)
- NGSA (Airbus) and fps (Boeing, 10-year ramp-up) were both launched in 2030. EIS is 2037 for NGSA and 2040 for fps. Both selected code 7: RR, P&W and CFM.
- Engine programmes: our UltraFan NB Solo (2030, ready 2037); P&W GTF2 Solo (2030, ready 2036); CFM ducted (ready 2036); CFM-Embraer partnership (ready 2037); GEnx upgrade (ready since 2033).
- No 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record.
- P&W said "We are making no Joint Venture commitment this round" (2030). It commits GTF2 for any airframer that selects it.
- Boeing: CFM is the baseline and certifies first. A P&W or RR engine follows in sequence once it shows maturity and durability.
- Airbus invites all three engine makers as risk-sharing partners.
- Our 2030 public word: "the Joint Venture is open to Pratt & Whitney, and we commit once its commitment is on the record."

OUR POSITION (brief)
- Hold is worth +30.07 (yield 127.3%).

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
I would change my view in seven cases.

(1) Watson reports that 2037 cannot be met without compressing testing. The date then moves, and we drop off NGSA: S2 becomes the base case and hold is +8.75. A 2035 Joint Venture that folds GTF2 (ready 2036) would then be the only route to NGSA, which makes me weigh the commit more, not less.

(2) Watson finds that a fold compresses testing or gives a Civil veto ground. The commit goes to hold at a declared $0.23B premium, and I would sign that.

(3) Evidence that the Joint Venture needs RR cash beyond its $4B share. I would re-price it, and it must still be at or above 0 in every column.

(4) The 2045 grid. I keep the standing commitment only if it is at or above withdrawing in every column.

(5) A 787 Re-engine naming UltraFan, or an A350 Re-engine, goes on the record. I would re-test the upgrade and UltraFan WB with the $5B strain stacked. Each must stay within its own bill or carry a premium within the caps.

(6) Delivered numbers show narrowbody early-unit or durability costs above the top of my $2-5B range, or a flying-hour shock threatens cash breakeven. I would re-phase and bring the buyback changes to the Board first.

(7) RR widebody share heads below 50%.
cfo.memo:
Safety first, then the balance sheet. Nothing here touches either.

I confirm Tufan's weights (0.65/0.10/0.05/0.10/0.05/0.05) and his numbers: Joint Venture +0.23, worst 0; cancel -33.63; cancel plus Joint Venture -30.16; upgrade -6.01; UltraFan WB -8.80. Hold is +27.34.

The Solo stays. Keeping it beats cancelling in every column, by 15.03 to 36.35, for $2.29B still to spend: about £0.84bn a year in 2035-36, roughly 9-12% of analyst free cash flow. Buybacks give way first. The dividend is not in play. No equity, no borrowing.

I co-sign the Joint Venture commit. It is never below hold: +2.28 in S4, which is the $2.29B of Solo spend we avoid, with our share unchanged at 36.5%. If Pratt & Whitney does not commit, nothing is spent. Last round's word is Tufan's to answer; on the numbers, holding costs $0.23B. A standing commitment needs a 2045 trigger: withdraw unless that grid shows it at or above withdrawing in every column.

I withhold on the upgrade and UltraFan WB. Each loses more than its own bill once the $5B strain is stacked on it.

Two things the grid does not show. Control's $4B line stays breached: $8.0B, or $5.7B in S4, and no order cures it. And the narrowbody ramp after 2037 will cost us: $2-5B on my range, more if durability bites. My record on launch economics is thin; that is inference.

That's how you should hold it. That's our best view at the minute.

ops.memo:
UltraFan NB, launched 2030, is ready 2037: zero margin against NGSA's 2037 entry into service, three years against fps 2040. Zero margin is a named pass, not a veto. The record shows no slip; gearbox sizing is the risk we test hardest. If the endurance test needs longer, the Committee hears it first and the date moves, not the test plan. A late engine drops us from NGSA; S2, -21.32, is the nearest measure.

Support: the Singapore-model partner MRO agreements (2034 gate) and the first partner shop with an EIS support team (2036 gate) are on plan. The board doesn't track them, so I re-commit them here. High-performing suppliers only. We go from 197 engines a year to 1,657 by 2040.

Joint Venture: no Civil ground. Formed in 2035, it folds GTF2 (2036) and our Solo (2037), so it is ready no later than 2037. Two conditions. It carries a folded engine on its own test plan; an UltraFan core with P&W's gearbox is a later engine with its own full programme. And we disclose no Joint Venture date. Structure is Tufan's call; I lean to partnership.

Widebody: 58% to 2041, 55.2% from 2042, every column. No widebody programme beside the narrowbody: $5B of strain, for good. Time on wing carries the Trent fleet inside budget.

Statement: clean, except "a partnership can still serve them", which implies a ready date. Say "the time to decide it is now".

We're pacing that program properly.

tests.name: Ready by EIS: UltraFan NB Solo (held)
tests.threshold: UltraFan NB ready at launch + 7 must be at or before the selecting airframe's EIS. Zero margin is a pass with a note, not a fail and not a veto ground. A late engine is a fail as advice, not a veto.

tests.name: Ready by EIS: Joint Venture, if P&W also commits in 2035
tests.threshold: The Joint Venture engine is ready at formation + 6, or earlier if a folded solo programme is further along. It must be ready by each live airframe's EIS. Formation must not compress any test plan.
tests.numbers:
On its own, formation 2035 + 6 = 2041. The rules make it earlier when a folded solo is further along. The folded programmes are GTF2 (2030 + 6 = ready 2036) and our Solo (2030 + 7 = ready 2037).

READY YEAR: no later than 2037, and 2036 if GTF2's date governs (inference; the bulletin shows the date only on formation). Against NGSA 2037: zero margin at worst, pass with a note. Against fps 2040: 3 years or more, pass. I CONFIRM the Board's reading, 'ready by 2037 at the latest'.

COMPRESSION: none on the board. The ready year is a folded programme's own launch + development years, so no test plan is shortened. In practice the risk is configuration. A merger two years before a zero-margin EIS must carry a folded engine on its own frozen test plan. An UltraFan core with P&W's gearbox is a new configuration: a new NPI with its own testing schedule, not a 2037 engine.

GEARBOX: P&W's gearbox could answer our gearbox-sizing constraint (dashboard_game.md §3). That is inference; I have no evidence of my own. It applies to the growth engine, through full testing.

FORMED IN 2045: formation comes after both EIS (2037, 2040) and would fold a ready, in-service Solo.

tests.threshold: No statement or disclosure of an EIS or ready date earlier than: launch + 7 for UltraFan NB (2037); launch + 6 for UltraFan WB; formation + 6 for the Joint Venture, or the earlier date the bulletin shows for a folded solo (none shown yet). Nothing on any airframer's dates.
tests.numbers:
Judged on the CEO's draft; to be re-checked at step 4.

- 'where we can be ready by its entry into service': clean.
- 'If testing needs longer, the date moves, not the test plan': clean.
- UltraFan WB: not ordered.
- Joint Venture: no date drafted. Formation + 6 = 2041 unless a folded programme is further along. The bulletin shows no folded date yet, so no Joint Venture date, explicit or implied, may be given.

ONE WORDING FIX: 'so this is the round a partnership can still serve them' implies a Joint Venture ready by 2037-2040, earlier than formation + 6 and before the bulletin shows it. Replace it with 'so if there is to be a partnership, the time to decide it is now.'

The statement names no airframer dates. The rationale must not present an UltraFan-core, P&W-gearbox engine as ready by 2037.

tests.name: Support before EIS
tests.threshold: RR has no narrowbody MRO scale (briefing constraint). A support plan through partner shops must exist before any narrowbody EIS, and it must be carried in any package with a narrowbody launch, trigger or commit (inference).
tests.numbers:
GATES OF RECORD (round 1 package; internal; inference):
(1) Singapore-model partner MRO agreements by 2034.
(2) The first partner shop inducting engines, and an EIS support team (field service, spares pool, repair technology), by 2036. That is one year before the 2037 EIS and four years before fps 2040.
(3) Narrowbody work only with high-performing suppliers (GBP 685m of GBP 2.5bn of external spend in 2023).

STATUS: on plan. The board neither prices nor tracks these gates, and the brief records no slip. So I report them on plan and re-commit them in this package; I claim no signature the record cannot show.

JOINT VENTURE: the commit is a narrowbody commit and needs the same plan before it goes in. If the Joint Venture forms, support moves to a joint network on the Singapore model: our partner shops plus the partner's in-service narrowbody shops (P&W flies the A320neo today, per rules.md; inference). A joint support agreement goes into the formation documents in 2035-36, before the first EIS in 2037. The package must carry this as a private other move.

tests.numbers:

Plan B (hold + commit to JV): strain $0. The Joint Venture is narrowbody and no widebody programme sits beside it. Overlap 0 years.

Plan E (upgrade launched 2035, counts 2038) beside the Solo, in development to 2037: 2 years of overlap (2035-37) and $5B of strain. Against hold: -6.03 / -6.03 / -6.02 / -6.03 / -5.87 / -5.87. Company red line.

Plan F (UltraFan WB launched 2035, ready 2041) beside the Solo: 2 years of overlap (2035-37) and $5B. Against hold: -9.00 in S1-S4, -6.96 in S5-S6. Red line: no Re-engine on the record, and the Solo is not 'both selected'.

CONFIRMED:
- Hold and the Joint Venture commit both carry $0.
- Once the Solo is ready in 2037, no cancel removes it. Any widebody programme from now on, beside the Solo or a formed Joint Venture, carries a permanent one-off $5B, whatever its dates.

NOTE: the integration work of a 2035 fold is not in the grid.

tests.name: Capacity and suppliers
tests.threshold: State RR engines a year from the brief's year table. The board sets no capacity limit, so the result is 'not applicable' unless the brief reports a constraint. Flag a narrowbody ramp as needing partner MRO and high-performing supplier capacity, as advice.
tests.numbers:
ENGINES A YEAR (hold or Joint Venture; S1 and S4-S6):
- NB: 965 (2037), 978 (2038), 990 (2039), then 1,460 a year from 2040 (36.5% of 4,000).
- WB: 197 to 2041, 188 from 2042.
- Total: 1,162 in 2037, 1,657 in 2040 and 1,648 from 2042, against 197 today. That is an 8.4x unit ramp.
- S2: 788 NB engines (19.7%). S3: 864 (21.6%).
- About 10,233 UltraFan NB engines delivered by end-2044 in S1.

Shop visits: I use my figure (1,100-1,200 a year at midterm, RX-0279), not the 1,400-1,500 definition.

No capacity limit on the board and none reported in the brief, so not applicable.

ADVICE: the ramp lands behind the widebody ramp and needs partner MRO and high-performing supplier capacity. A Joint Venture changes the plan. In S4, shares are equalised with P&W, and support is shared on the Singapore model through the partner's narrowbody shops. That reduces the MRO build we carry alone (inference).

tests.name: Widebody dominance
tests.threshold: RR widebody engine share of at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 on the brief's projection. Time on wing is the lever (inference).
tests.numbers:
RR WB share on hold, and on hold + Joint Venture: 58.0% in 2040, 55.2% in 2045 and 55.2% in 2050 (the GEnx upgrade counts from 2042), in every column S1-S6. The lowest is 55.2%, 5.2 points above the line.
- The upgrade would give 60.0% in 2050.
- UltraFan WB would give 64.8%, in S5-S6 only.
- Test not triggered.

S5 EXPOSURE: Airbus's WB airframe share falls from 41.2% to 30.2% by 2050 (787 Re-engine alone). We power the A350 alone, and we are sole source on 3 platforms (RX-0292), so that is the franchise to watch, even though the board's engine share does not move.

PROPOSED OTHER MOVE (unpriced; public or private, the CEO's call): a Trent time-on-wing programme inside the existing fleet budget.
- Longer-life HP turbine blades on the Trent 1000 and 7000.
- Life extension for life-limited parts.
- UltraFan technology inserted into the Trent fleet.
- Trent XWB shop-visit cost down.
It is not the `t1000_upgrade` order and not a new programme, so it carries no strain.

tests.numbers: The Solo is held. UltraFan's geared-architecture technology (25% more efficient than the first Trent) keeps feeding time on wing on today's Trent fleet. If the Solo folds in S4, its technology stays with RR and still flows to the fleet: a 2-way flow. Qualitative; grid unchanged.

It is the company's cancel red line and the Board's veto, not mine.

Our technology comes into it: 'we are actually bringing a technology' [RX-0072]. No terms, no ready date and no airframer date are disclosed.

other_moves.move: Joint narrowbody support plan before first EIS (Watson)
other_moves.detail: Last round's gates are re-committed. Watson reports them on plan; the board does not track them, so no signature is claimed beyond the record. (1) Singapore-model partner MRO agreements, gate 2034. (2) First partner shop inducting engines and an EIS support team (field service, spares pool, repair technology) by 2036, ahead of a first EIS no earlier than 2037. (3) Narrowbody work only with high-performing suppliers. If the Joint Venture forms, a joint support agreement goes into the formation documents in 2035-36, before the first EIS: our partner shops plus the partner's in-service narrowbody shops. A folded programme carries on its own frozen test plan. An UltraFan-core, P&W-gearbox configuration would be a later engine with its own full programme, not a 2037 engine. Internal gates; inference; not disclosed.

other_moves.move: Funding plan for the remaining Solo spend and the narrowbody ramp (McCabe)
other_moves.detail: About $2.29B (about £1.7bn, roughly £0.84bn a year in 2035-36) remains on the Solo, about 9-12% of analyst free cash flow. Any need beyond buybacks comes back to the Board before it arises.

We keep the commitment only if that round's grid shows it at or above withdraw in every column, with the worst column at or above 0, no premium needed, and no disruption to support of the in-service UltraFan NB fleet (about 10,000 engines by end-2044 in S1). The test is run on the 2045 grid before P&W's move is known. No options management [RX-0051].

other_moves.detail: Longer-life HP turbine blades on the Trent 1000 and Trent 7000, life extension for life-limited parts, UltraFan technology inserted into the Trent fleet, and Trent XWB shop-visit cost down. Funded inside the existing fleet budget. It is not the `t1000_upgrade` order and not a new programme, and it carries no strain. No dates disclosed.

other_moves.move: Commercial terms with Airbus and Boeing
other_moves.detail: We answer Airbus's invitation on NGSA and Boeing's code-7 engine competition on fps on standard commercial terms: value remunerated, win-win, with no launch-style concessions to hold a selection. Every new contract goes through the Investment Committee [RX-0081, RX-0097, R-1582]. We will show the maturity and durability Boeing's sequence asks for, and we do not speak for any airframer's dates.

decision.public_statement: So, plainly. UltraFan narrowbody stays on plan: ready no earlier than seven years from launch, with support in place before entry into service. If testing needs longer, the date moves, not the test plan. Both airframers have selected all three engine makers, Pratt & Whitney included. So if there is to be a partnership, the time to decide it is now. Last time we said we would commit once Pratt & Whitney's commitment was on the record. Frankly, with decisions made at the same time, waiting for that means deciding too late. So our Joint Venture commitment is on the record today, on one condition: it forms only if Pratt & Whitney commits too. If not, nothing is spent, and we will not hold it open. We don't need partnership for capability, but our preference is that. We launch for any airframer that selects us where we can be ready by its entry into service. Widebody is our core: no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody, and Trent time on wing keeps improving. We won't do anything not profitable. When we commit, we deliver.
decision.rationale:
DECISION
- `ultrafan_nb_solo: hold`
- `jv_with_pw: commit`
- `ultrafan_wb: hold`
- `t1000_upgrade: hold`
This is my framing proposal unchanged. Both memos recommend the same orders. Only the public statement changes, to take Watson's wording fix. The one Board item is the Joint Venture commit. Everything else stays at the default.

GRID (the Board's matched rows, S1-S6)
- "UltraFan NB: hold + commit to JV": +30.07 / +8.75 / +18.26 / +32.35 / +29.98 / +29.98.
- "UltraFan NB: hold": +30.07 / +8.75 / +18.26 / +30.07 / +29.98 / +29.98.
- Gain: 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.28 / 0 / 0. Worst column 0, against a $4B bill.
- Weights (McCabe confirmed them) S1-S6: 0.65 / 0.10 / 0.05 / 0.10 / 0.05 / 0.05.
  - Expected PV +27.57 against +27.34, a gain of +0.23.
  - At the Board's illustration (0.50, then 0.10 each): +26.97 against +26.74, also +0.23.
  - The commit is at or above hold in every column, so the verdict holds under any weights.
- Rows struck, gain over hold at my weights (worst column):
  - cancel: -33.63 (-36.35);
  - cancel + Joint Venture: -30.16 (-36.35; -4.00 against "hold + commit to JV" in S4);
  - Trent 1000 upgrade: -6.01 (-6.03);
  - UltraFan WB: -8.80 (-9.00).

WHY THE SOLO STAYS
Keeping the Solo beats a cancel in every column, by 15.03 to 36.35. Both live airframes carry code 7, and the engine is ready in 2037, by NGSA's 2037 EIS and fps's 2040. It is not an orphan, so a cancel breaks the company rule [R-1573]. This is the last round a cancel is possible; it is closed. When we commit, we deliver [RX-0124].

WHY THE JOINT VENTURE NOW: rebutting last round's word and the ExCo's 'P&W first' default
Last round I said publicly that "we commit once its commitment is on the record". The ExCo's team default is partner first once P&W has committed. I am departing from the letter of both, for four reasons.
(1) Orders are sealed and simultaneous. P&W's commitment can reach the record only a round after it is made, so waiting means committing in 2045 at the earliest. By then NGSA (2037) and fps (2040) are in service, and a fold would write off about $4B of a ready engine. The word would defeat its own purpose.
(2) The substance of the word survives. Its point was no Joint Venture without a partner and an airframe. Under the rules the Joint Venture forms only in a round when P&W is also committed. Both live airframes carry code 7, which includes P&W, and that meets the Board's partner limb [R-1010]. If P&W does not commit, nothing forms and nothing is spent.
(3) The fold condition I set last round is met: the fold row beats keeping the Solo in S4 and ties it elsewhere.
(4) It is a choice with a trigger, not options management [RX-0051]: withdraw in 2045 by default. It is the same logic as last round's `launch_if_selected`.
The Board said it would not ask me to break a public word for +$0.23B. I am not breaking it for the money. I am squaring it in public, in today's statement, and giving the reason. "There's no change of strategy" [RX-0098]: partnership is our stated preference [RX-0118]. Last round I said publicly that "we commit once its commitment is on the record". The ExCo's team default is partner first once P&W has committed. I am departing from the letter of both, for four reasons.
(1) Orders are sealed and simultaneous. P&W's commitment can reach the record only a round after it is made, so waiting means committing in 2045 at the earliest. By then NGSA (2037) and fps (2040) are in service, and a fold would write off about $4B of a ready engine. The word would defeat its own purpose.
(2) The substance of the word survives. Its point was no Joint Venture without a partner and an airframe. Under the rules the Joint Venture forms only in a round when P&W is also committed. Both live airframes carry code 7, which includes P&W, and that meets the Board's partner limb [R-1010]. If P&W does not commit, nothing forms and nothing is spent.
(3) The fold condition I set last round is met: the fold row beats keeping the Solo in S4 and ties it elsewhere.
(4) It is a choice with a trigger, not options management [RX-0051]: withdraw in 2045 by default. It is the same logic as last round's `launch_if_selected`.
The Board said it would not ask me to break a public word for +$0.23B. I am not breaking it for the money. I am squaring it in public, in today's statement, and giving the reason. "There's no change of strategy" [RX-0098]: partnership is our stated preference [RX-0118]. On cash, the +2.28 in S4 is in substance the $2.29B of Solo spend avoided, with our narrowbody share unchanged at 36.5% in 2050.

MATURITY: no claim of a new engine by 2037
A Joint Venture formed in 2035 folds GTF2 (ready 2036) and our Solo (ready 2037). It carries a folded engine on its own frozen test plan, ready no later than 2037 on the board's rule; Watson confirms it. I do not count on an UltraFan-core, P&W-gearbox engine in service by 2037. That configuration would be a later engine with its own full programme. No Joint Venture date is disclosed.

VETO CHECKS
- McCabe co-signs the commit: worst column 0; capex £0.84bn a year on hold, £0 in S4 after the fold; funded from free cash flow, buybacks giving way first.
- Her binding withholds (the upgrade, UltraFan WB, a cancel paired with the commit) all apply to orders I do not give.
- No balance-sheet ground arises.
- Watson invokes no Civil veto. I have met the three grounds he reserved for step 4:
  (a) No Joint Venture ready date, explicit or implied. I struck 'a partnership can still serve them' and used his wording, 'if there is to be a partnership, the time to decide it is now'. No UltraFan NB date before 2037. Nothing on airframer dates.
  (b) No claim of a new configuration by 2037.
  (c) The joint partner-shop support plan before the first EIS is carried as a private other move.
- Red-line flags: none stands. The cancel, the upgrade and UltraFan WB are all struck. Strain stays at $0. `overrides` is empty.

PREMIUM
$0. The submitted plan is the best expected grid plan, and no item is held below the best plan.

CONTROL'S METRICS (own NB money / strain / RR WB share 2050 / RR NB share 2050)
- S1: $8.0B / $0 / 55.2% / 36.5%
- S2: $8.0B / $0 / 55.2% / 19.7%

Expected own NB money: $7.77B. Stated plainly: no order this round brings it within $4B. Hold leaves $8.0B, a cancel $5.7B, and a fold in S4 $5.7B. The cause is the 2030 trigger on a double selection. We never cancel or fold for the metric alone.

2045 PLAN
If our commitment stands and P&W commits only in 2045, the Joint Venture would form after both airframes are in service. A ready Solo would then fold, with about $4B written off and shares equalised. So the 2045 default is `withdraw`, unless that round's grid shows the commit at or above withdraw in every column, the worst column at or above 0, and fleet support undisturbed. Both McCabe and Watson back this.

DOCTRINE NOTE
My own record is Medium on narrowbody launch behaviour and Low on Joint Venture terms. The partner test, the 2045 trigger and the ramp ranges are doctrine and McCabe's numbers, not my record.

recommendations.text: Maturity and support, our absolute priority. A 2037 entry into service at NGSA is zero margin, and gearbox sizing is the named risk. Watson should report the gearbox endurance and durability results to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee every quarter until 2037. If 2037 cannot be met without compressing testing, he tells the Committee first; the date moves, never the test plan. He reports the support gates 'on plan' while saying they are not tracked. We want their status reported with evidence: partner MRO agreements (2034), and the first partner shop with an EIS support team (2036). If the Joint Venture forms, the joint support agreement must be in the formation documents before 2037. The folded engine flies on its own frozen test plan, with no reconfiguration before EIS. An UltraFan-core, P&W-gearbox engine comes to the board as a new programme with its own full test plan. Before fps in 2040, show Boeing's sequence the full test plan complete, life-limited parts at full life and NGSA in-service durability data.

The Joint Venture forward plan. The commitment stands until withdrawn. In the 2045 round, bring the withdraw row against the keep row, column by column. The default is `withdraw`, unless keeping it is at or above withdraw in every column, with the worst column at or above 0, no premium, and support of the in-service UltraFan NB fleet undisturbed. Confirm from the 2045 brief how a same-round withdraw is adjudicated against a P&W commit. A fold of a ready engine would write off about $4B, gain nothing on Control's metric, and could disturb fleet support. If the Joint Venture forms this round, report the $1.71B fold write-off as non-cash, on spend already made. Any request for RR money beyond our $4B share comes back to the board before it arises.

Funding order: reconcile McCabe's correction before the board pack goes out. Buybacks give way first, as in 2015. The 30-40% dividend ranks after the balance sheet in our capital frame. The remaining Solo spend (about $2.29B, about £0.84bn a year in 2035-36, 9-12% of analyst free cash flow) belongs to a selected programme in delivery, not new programme spend. It is not to be re-phased in any way that moves the date or compresses testing. Any step beyond buybacks, on the dividend or on programme phasing, comes to the board before it arises. McCabe should report quarterly, including the narrowbody ramp after 2037. That ramp is not in the grid: $2-5B is her base case, planned at the top, and about $10B her reasonable worst case.

The widebody core and Control's strain line. Strain stays at $0. From 2037 the Solo can no longer be cancelled, so every future widebody item will carry the $5B strain on top of its own bill, and we will judge it that way. If a 787 or A350 Re-engine goes on the record (S5, S6), or RR widebody share heads toward 50%, bring the upgrade and UltraFan WB rows next round with the strain shown and the premium caps applied ($3B in all, at most $1B for UltraFan WB). Trent time on wing inside the existing budget is the right defence now. Watch the A350 sole-source exposure: Airbus widebody airframe share falls to 30.2% in S5, even though the board's engine share holds at 55.2%.

Control's terms and the public word. Keep stating plainly that our own narrowbody money is $8.0B ($5.7B only if P&W commits) against $4B. The cause is the 2030 double selection, and we never cancel or fold for the metric alone. The statement is clean on disclosure: no early date, no Joint Venture date, nothing on airframer dates. Next round, say plainly where the Joint Venture stands once P&W's 2035 orders are published, and do not describe a Joint Venture engine as able to serve either airframe before the bulletin shows a ready date. Answer Airbus's risk-sharing invitation and Boeing's code-7 competition on standard commercial terms, with no launch-style concessions to hold a selection.

board_review.note: The board approves. Product safety is and always must be our most important priority, and nothing here compresses it. The Solo stays on its own test plan, ready 2037. A Joint Venture formed this round folds an engine ready no later than 2037, with no date disclosed and support in place first. The commitment is never below hold: +2.28 in S4 and 0 elsewhere, worst case 0 against a $4B bill. It spends nothing unless Pratt & Whitney commits too. McCabe co-signs and Watson raises no veto. The chief executive has squared last round's word in public, and he has our support. We note openly that our own narrowbody money stands at $8.0B against Control's $4B. No order cures that, and we will not cancel or fold for the metric. Zero margin at NGSA is the risk we do not underestimate. In 2045 we expect a withdraw unless that grid shows it pays.
